Chapter 1

From particles to bulk behavior

A glass of water has temperature, pressure, viscosity, and surface tension. These properties describe distributions and responses of molecules, rather than attributes of an isolated molecule. Their usefulness depends on averaging over enough microscopic motion while retaining the quantities that control the experiment.

Temperature and entropy describe energy exchange and the statistical weight of macroscopic states. Pressure, diffusion, sound, and viscosity follow the transport of conserved quantities. Elasticity and surface tension describe the cost of deformation, while screening shows how the surrounding material modifies a perturbing field. Hydrodynamics combines these ideas: it retains slowly varying fields, constrains their evolution by conservation, and represents faster processes through an equation of state and transport coefficients. This change of description can be effective far from any phase transition.

01Temperature and thermal equilibrium

A gas thermometer and a metal thermometer have different microscopic degrees of freedom, yet they agree after equilibrating with the same bath. Their agreement follows from the quantity that energy exchange equalizes. It need not imply equal energies per particle: rotations, vibrations, interactions, and quantum level spacings all affect how a body stores energy.

Consider two weakly coupled bodies with fixed combined energy EEE. Let ΩA(EA)\Omega_A(E_A)ΩA​(EA​) count states in a narrow energy interval compatible with the other constraints on AAA, and write SA=kBln⁡ΩAS_A=k_B\ln\Omega_ASA​=kB​lnΩA​, where kBk_BkB​ is Boltzmann's constant. Neglecting the interaction energy, the combined state count is proportional to ΩA(EA)ΩB(E−EA)\Omega_A(E_A)\Omega_B(E-E_A)ΩA​(EA​)ΩB​(E−EA​). At a stable maximum,

∂SA∂EA=∂SB∂EB,1T=(∂S∂E)V,N.\frac{\partial S_A}{\partial E_A}=\frac{\partial S_B}{\partial E_B},\qquad \frac1T=\left(\frac{\partial S}{\partial E}\right)_{V,N}.∂EA​∂SA​​=∂EB​∂SB​​,T1​=(∂E∂S​)V,N​.

Volume VVV and particle number NNN are held fixed in the derivative. Reciprocal temperature is the entropy slope. For macroscopic bodies with ordinary stable thermodynamics, the state count is sharply concentrated near this maximum, making temperature reproducible despite microscopic fluctuations.

For a small system in a much larger bath, expanding the bath entropy gives SB(E−Ei)≃SB(E)−Ei/TS_B(E-E_i)\simeq S_B(E)-E_i/TSB​(E−Ei​)≃SB​(E)−Ei​/T. Its number of compatible bath states is therefore proportional to e−Ei/(kBT)e^{-E_i/(k_BT)}e−Ei​/(kB​T), the Boltzmann weight of system state iii. The same temperature governs a gas's velocity distribution and a spin's level populations because both exchange energy with the bath. A thermometer measures a property calibrated against this parameter.

This reasoning requires equilibration of the relevant degrees of freedom. In a driven material, electrons and lattice vibrations may exchange energy slowly enough to have different effective temperatures. A single reading then characterizes only the degrees of freedom to which the instrument responds.

References
  • Tong, Statistical Physics, §1.2.2 and §1.3. Entropy maximization, thermal equilibrium, and the canonical distribution.

02Pressure as momentum transfer

A piston receives separate molecular impacts but feels a nearly steady force. In the local rest frame of an equilibrium fluid, pressure is the normal momentum transferred per unit area and time, averaged over scales large compared with individual collisions. A moving fluid also carries momentum through a surface by bulk advection; this contribution must be separated from pressure.

Take NNN noninteracting particles of mass mmm in a rectangular box of volume VVV. A particle with normal velocity vxv_xvx​ transfers 2m∣vx∣2m|v_x|2m∣vx​∣ when it reflects from a wall. It returns after 2Lx/∣vx∣2L_x/|v_x|2Lx​/∣vx​∣, where LxL_xLx​ is the box length. Summing the average force and dividing by wall area gives

p=NmV⟨vx2⟩=Nm3V⟨v2⟩.p=\frac{Nm}{V}\langle v_x^2\rangle=\frac{Nm}{3V}\langle v^2\rangle.p=VNm​⟨vx2​⟩=3VNm​⟨v2⟩.

The second equality assumes an isotropic velocity distribution. Classical thermal equilibrium gives m⟨v2⟩=3kBTm\langle v^2\rangle=3k_BTm⟨v2⟩=3kB​T, hence pV=NkBTpV=Nk_BTpV=NkB​T. Number density and temperature determine the average momentum flux, although the sequence of impacts remains irregular.

The same accounting applies across an imaginary plane inside the gas: particles crossing it exchange momentum between neighboring regions. Interparticle forces also transmit momentum across such a plane. They contribute substantially in a dense liquid, where the ideal-gas formula no longer applies. In equilibrium, the mechanical pressure agrees with p=−(∂F/∂V)T,Np=-(\partial F/\partial V)_{T,N}p=−(∂F/∂V)T,N​, where the Helmholtz free energy F=E−TSF=E-TSF=E−TS gives the reversible work of changing volume at fixed temperature.

A scalar pressure describes isotropic normal stress. A sheared fluid or a solid generally requires a stress tensor, whose component σij\sigma_{ij}σij​ is the force in direction iii per area across a surface normal to direction jjj. Small sensors also resolve fluctuations hidden by macroscopic averaging. Thus the familiar pressure of a gas is a particularly simple form of the more general transport of momentum.

References
  • Feynman, Leighton and Sands, The Feynman Lectures on Physics, I §39–2. Molecular momentum transfer and the ideal-gas equation of state.

03Entropy and the direction of relaxation

Remove a partition confining a gas to half a box. The gas spreads, although reversing all particle momenta would reverse the microscopic trajectory. The statistical explanation concerns how much phase space corresponds to each macroscopic description and how the gas was prepared.

A macrostate specifies quantities such as particle counts in spatial cells. A classical microstate specifies all positions and momenta. Boltzmann entropy is SB=kBln⁡ΩS_B=k_B\ln\OmegaSB​=kB​lnΩ, where Ω\OmegaΩ is the phase-space volume compatible with a macrostate, measured in fixed microscopic units. For an ideal gas expanding freely into twice its initial volume, the available positional volume gains a factor 2N2^N2N, so

ΔSB=NkBln⁡2.\Delta S_B=Nk_B\ln 2.ΔSB​=NkB​ln2.

At equilibrium, independently distributed particle positions put all NNN particles in the original half with probability 2−N2^{-N}2−N. This explains why that macrostate is rarely observed; the relaxation time still depends on the dynamics.

The Boltzmann entropy of a macrostate must be distinguished from the fine-grained Gibbs entropy of a distribution. For probability density ρ\rhoρ on phase space with volume element dΓd\GammadΓ, Hamiltonian evolution preserves −kB∫ρln⁡ρ dΓ-k_B\int\rho\ln\rho\,d\Gamma−kB​∫ρlnρdΓ, with a fixed reference measure understood. The distribution develops fine structure and correlations that a macroscopic density measurement does not resolve. For an isolated quantum system, unitary evolution similarly preserves the full-state von Neumann entropy, while a subsystem's entropy can grow through entanglement.

Ordinary relaxation starts from an unusually small region of phase space and evolves toward macrostates occupying much more of it. This argument needs dynamics that actually explores the relevant regions: conserved quantities and restricted motion can prevent equilibration. Reversing an expansion would require preparing the detailed position–momentum correlations generated during its history. Matching the total energy and density alone would not reproduce that exceptional preparation.

References
  • Tong, Statistical Physics, §1.2.1 and §1.3.3. Boltzmann and Gibbs entropy and their different statistical meanings.

04Diffusion from random motion

A dye spot spreads because more molecules cross from a concentrated region into a dilute one than cross back. Individual molecules need no directional bias. A simple model makes the resulting law explicit: a walker takes independent steps +a+a+a or −a-a−a every time interval τ\tauτ, each with probability 1/21/21/2.

The position distribution obeys a discrete update that averages its two neighboring values. Expanding for variation over distances much larger than aaa and times much longer than τ\tauτ gives

∂tP=D∂x2P,D=a22τ,⟨x2⟩=2Dt.\partial_tP=D\partial_x^2P,\qquad D=\frac{a^2}{2\tau},\qquad \langle x^2\rangle=2Dt.∂t​P=D∂x2​P,D=2τa2​,⟨x2⟩=2Dt.

Here the walker starts at the origin, P(x,t)P(x,t)P(x,t) is its probability density, and DDD has units of area per time. A localized initial distribution approaches a Gaussian whose width grows as t\sqrt{t}t​. Transport across twice the distance therefore takes roughly four times as long.

For many particles, conservation gives ∂tc+∇⋅j=0\partial_tc+\nabla\cdot\mathbf j=0∂t​c+∇⋅j=0, where ccc is number concentration and j\mathbf jj is particle flux. Fick's constitutive law, j=−D∇c\mathbf j=-D\nabla cj=−D∇c, closes this equation and reproduces diffusion for constant DDD. In an interacting mixture, the more general driving quantity is chemical potential, the free-energy change per added particle. Its gradient need not point along the concentration gradient.

Ordinary diffusion requires microscopic memory to decay sufficiently quickly. Before velocity correlations decay, motion can be ballistic, with mean squared displacement proportional to t2t^2t2. Persistent correlations or broad waiting-time distributions can instead produce anomalous diffusion, for which that displacement is not proportional to time. Flow and reactions add further transport and source terms. An observed slow expansion should therefore be tested over a range of times before assigning it a small constant diffusivity.

05Sound as a collective density wave

A spoken word crosses a room without carrying the speaker's air along with it. The propagating disturbance consists of local compression and velocity changes. A pressure excess accelerates adjacent fluid, whose motion creates the next compression.

Write density and pressure as ρ0+δρ\rho_0+\delta\rhoρ0​+δρ and p0+δpp_0+\delta pp0​+δp about uniform equilibrium, and let v\mathbf vv be the small mean velocity. To first order, mass and momentum conservation give

∂tδρ+ρ0∇⋅v=0,ρ0∂tv=−∇δp.\partial_t\delta\rho+\rho_0\nabla\cdot\mathbf v=0,\qquad \rho_0\partial_t\mathbf v=-\nabla\delta p.∂t​δρ+ρ0​∇⋅v=0,ρ0​∂t​v=−∇δp.

When heat transfer between neighboring compressed and expanded regions is negligible within a cycle, the response is approximately adiabatic. The equation of state then gives δp=cs2δρ\delta p=c_s^2\delta\rhoδp=cs2​δρ, with cs2=(∂p/∂ρ)sc_s^2=(\partial p/\partial\rho)_scs2​=(∂p/∂ρ)s​ and sss the entropy per unit mass. Combining the equations yields ∂t2δρ=cs2∇2δρ\partial_t^2\delta\rho=c_s^2\nabla^2\delta\rho∂t2​δρ=cs2​∇2δρ.

For an ideal gas, cs2=γp0/ρ0c_s^2=\gamma p_0/\rho_0cs2​=γp0​/ρ0​, where γ=Cp/CV\gamma=C_p/C_Vγ=Cp​/CV​ is the heat-capacity ratio. More generally, sound speed compares the stiffness against compression with the inertia of the fluid. A dense material can transmit sound rapidly if it is correspondingly difficult to compress. The wave's wavelength describes the coordinated density pattern, not the distance traveled by an individual molecule.

Local equilibrium must be established faster than the oscillation, and a wavelength must be large compared with microscopic transport lengths. Viscosity and heat conduction then give small attenuation corrections. Large amplitudes change the local propagation speed and can steepen a wave into a shock. These corrections connect the ideal wave equation to the same momentum and energy transport processes that underlie diffusion and viscosity.

References
  • Feynman, Leighton and Sands, The Feynman Lectures on Physics, I Ch. 47. Acoustic wave equation and the adiabatic sound speed.

06Viscosity and the diffusion of momentum

Moving one plate past another with fluid between them requires a force even when the plates never touch. Faster fluid layers transfer momentum to slower neighbors. For a Newtonian fluid, the resulting viscous stress is linear in the local rate of deformation.

In simple shear,

σxy=η ∂yvx.\sigma_{xy}=\eta\,\partial_yv_x.σxy​=η∂y​vx​.

Here vxv_xvx​ is velocity along the plates, yyy measures distance across the gap, and σxy\sigma_{xy}σxy​ is tangential stress across a surface normal to yyy. The dynamic shear viscosity η\etaη has units of pascal seconds. Steady flow between plates of area AAA, separation hhh, and relative speed UUU, with no slip at either plate and no imposed pressure gradient, has a linear velocity profile and requires force F=ηAU/hF=\eta AU/hF=ηAU/h.

In a dilute gas, molecules transport momentum between collisions, giving the estimate η∼ρvthℓ\eta\sim\rho v_{\rm th}\ellη∼ρvth​ℓ. Here ρ\rhoρ is mass density, vthv_{\rm th}vth​ a thermal speed, and ℓ\ellℓ the mean free path. Increasing density shortens ℓ\ellℓ, approximately compensating for the larger number of momentum carriers. In a dense liquid, intermolecular forces and structural rearrangements dominate the relaxation instead. Different microscopic mechanisms can therefore produce the same leading stress law.

In this shear flow, the work becomes heat at rate η(∂yvx)2\eta(\partial_yv_x)^2η(∂y​vx​)2 per volume. Momentum disturbances spread with kinematic viscosity ν=η/ρ\nu=\eta/\rhoν=η/ρ, which has the same dimensions as a diffusion coefficient. A polymer solution may retain stress after the motion stops because stretched molecules relax slowly. Such memory requires a time-dependent constitutive relation; a constant viscosity is adequate only when those internal relaxations are fast compared with the experiment.

References
  • Feynman, Leighton and Sands, The Feynman Lectures on Physics, II §41–1 and §41–2. Shear viscosity and the viscous stress tensor.
  • Feynman, Leighton and Sands, The Feynman Lectures on Physics, I Ch. 43. Kinetic estimates for molecular momentum transport.

07Elasticity and persistent constraints

A metal rod returns nearly to its initial length after a small pull because deforming its collective atomic arrangement raises the free energy. Its atoms continue to vibrate throughout. Elasticity describes displacements relative to a stable reference configuration, on time scales over which irreversible rearrangements are negligible.

Let u(r)\mathbf u(\mathbf r)u(r) be the displacement of material initially at r\mathbf rr. The small-strain tensor ϵij=(∂iuj+∂jui)/2\epsilon_{ij}=(\partial_i u_j+\partial_j u_i)/2ϵij​=(∂i​uj​+∂j​ui​)/2 measures changes of lengths and angles while removing infinitesimal rigid rotations. Expanding about an unstressed configuration gives

F−F0=12∫Cijklϵijϵkl dV,σij=Cijklϵkl.F-F_0=\frac12\int C_{ijkl}\epsilon_{ij}\epsilon_{kl}\,dV,\qquad \sigma_{ij}=C_{ijkl}\epsilon_{kl}.F−F0​=21​∫Cijkl​ϵij​ϵkl​dV,σij​=Cijkl​ϵkl​.

Repeated indices are summed. The elastic stiffness tensor CijklC_{ijkl}Cijkl​ relates strain to stress; σij\sigma_{ij}σij​ is force in direction iii per area across a surface normal to jjj. A linear stress law follows from a quadratic expansion of free energy, even when the underlying atomic forces are nonlinear.

For an isotropic solid, two moduli suffice: the bulk modulus penalizes volume change and the shear modulus penalizes distortion at fixed volume. Crystal symmetry generally permits additional independent coefficients. These coefficients include thermal effects as well as bond energetics. In rubber, stretching a polymer network reduces the number of accessible chain configurations, so much of the restoring force is entropic.

An ordinary liquid continually rearranges under sustained shear; a solid retains a restoring stress on the measurement time scale. A material may therefore respond elastically during a rapid pull but flow under a slow load. Glasses achieve finite-time rigidity without periodic atomic order, while defects and bond rearrangements allow permanent deformation at larger loads. The elastic field remains useful as long as its reference configuration persists through the experiment.

References
  • Feynman, Leighton and Sands, The Feynman Lectures on Physics, II Ch. 39. Elastic stiffness, strain energy, and the limits of linear elasticity.
  • MIT, Electronic and Mechanical Properties of Materials, Elasticity lectures. Bonding and entropic contributions to elastic response.

08Surface tension and curved interfaces

A small free drop tends to become spherical because creating liquid–vapor interface costs free energy. Surface molecules have different surroundings from molecules in the interior. The resulting surface tension γ\gammaγ is the reversible free-energy cost per added area under specified thermodynamic conditions.

For a clean interface with approximately constant γ\gammaγ, its free-energy contribution is Fs=γAF_s=\gamma AFs​=γA. A spherical drop of radius RRR has dA=8πR dRdA=8\pi R\,dRdA=8πRdR and dV=4πR2 dRdV=4\pi R^2\,dRdV=4πR2dR. Balancing surface work against the pressure difference gives

Δp dV=γ dA,Δp=2γR.\Delta p\,dV=\gamma\,dA,\qquad \Delta p=\frac{2\gamma}{R}.ΔpdV=γdA,Δp=R2γ​.

This Young–Laplace relation says that the interior pressure is higher, with a greater jump for a smaller drop. It applies to one spherical interface; a thin soap bubble has two. At a general smooth interface, the pressure jump is γ\gammaγ times the sum of its two principal curvatures, with signs fixed by the chosen normal.

At fixed volume, a sphere minimizes surface area. Gravity becomes competitive over the capillary length ℓc=γ/(Δρg)\ell_c=\sqrt{\gamma/(\Delta\rho g)}ℓc​=γ/(Δρg)​, where Δρ\Delta\rhoΔρ is the density difference between phases and ggg gravitational acceleration. Small drops are therefore rounded, while larger ones can be strongly deformed by gravity. On a solid substrate, the free energies of the solid–liquid and solid–vapor interfaces also determine the equilibrium contact angle.

Surface tension includes both energetic and entropic effects. Molecules that accumulate at an interface can alter it; spatial gradients of γ\gammaγ exert tangential stresses and drive flow. The treatment of an interface as a sharp surface with a constant coefficient becomes inaccurate when the drop radius approaches the molecular interfacial thickness.

References
  • MIT, Advanced Fluid Dynamics, Section 11: Surface Tension. Surface free energy, capillary forces, and wetting.
  • Bush, Interfacial Phenomena, Lecture 3: Fluid Statics. Curvature–pressure balance and the capillary length.

09Screening by mobile charges

A charge in an electrolyte attracts opposite ions and repels ions of the same sign. Their redistribution weakens its field at large distances. The measured potential therefore belongs to the inserted charge together with the response of the medium.

Consider ions of charges +q+q+q and −q-q−q, each with bulk number density n0n_0n0​, in a solvent of permittivity ε\varepsilonε. At temperature TTT, dilute-ion Boltzmann distributions give n±=n0exp⁡(∓qϕ/kBT)n_\pm=n_0\exp(\mp q\phi/k_BT)n±​=n0​exp(∓qϕ/kB​T) in potential ϕ\phiϕ. For ∣qϕ∣≪kBT|q\phi|\ll k_BT∣qϕ∣≪kB​T, the induced charge density is q(n+−n−)≃−2n0q2ϕ/(kBT)q(n_+-n_-)\simeq-2n_0q^2\phi/(k_BT)q(n+​−n−​)≃−2n0​q2ϕ/(kB​T). Outside the inserted charge, Poisson's equation becomes

∇2ϕ=ϕλD2,λD=εkBT2n0q2.\nabla^2\phi=\frac{\phi}{\lambda_D^2},\qquad \lambda_D=\sqrt{\frac{\varepsilon k_BT}{2n_0q^2}}.∇2ϕ=λD2​ϕ​,λD​=2n0​q2εkB​T​​.

The Debye length λD\lambda_DλD​ measures the screening distance. In three dimensions, linear response to a point charge QQQ gives ϕ(r)=Qe−r/λD/(4πεr)\phi(r)=Qe^{-r/\lambda_D}/(4\pi\varepsilon r)ϕ(r)=Qe−r/λD​/(4πεr). At fixed permittivity and density, higher temperature weakens the ionic concentration around the source and lengthens the screening distance. More mobile ions shorten it.

The calculation is self-consistent: the potential changes the ion distribution, and the redistributed ions contribute to that same potential. Using the bare charge's potential throughout would miss this feedback. In the infinite-medium solution, the integrated induced charge compensates QQQ; finite systems must also satisfy their boundary and total-charge constraints.

For a point source, linearization necessarily fails sufficiently close to the origin. The exponential expression describes the weak-field region; a nonlinear core can change its amplitude. Finite ion sizes and strong ionic correlations can further invalidate the dilute mean-field treatment. Metals screen through quantum electronic occupations and may have oscillatory responses, so screening in general need not have the Debye form.

References
  • Hutchinson, Introduction to Plasma Physics I, §1.2.3: Debye Shielding. Debye shielding in dilute plasma; the two-mobile-species coefficient is derived here.

10Hydrodynamics from slow conserved fields

Density, velocity, and temperature can predict large-scale fluid motion without specifying molecular coordinates. Conservation explains why these fields remain important: a conserved quantity leaves a region through its boundary, so a fluctuation spread over a long distance generally relaxes slowly.

For a one-component fluid, mass, momentum, and energy provide the basic fields. Local equilibrium assumes that microscopic degrees of freedom relax within a region much smaller than the scale of macroscopic variation. An equilibrium equation of state then relates local pressure, density, and temperature. With mass density ρ\rhoρ and local mean velocity v\mathbf vv, mass conservation is ∂tρ+∇⋅(ρv)=0\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot(\rho\mathbf v)=0∂t​ρ+∇⋅(ρv)=0.

For an incompressible Newtonian fluid with constant mass density ρ\rhoρ and shear viscosity η\etaη, momentum balance becomes

ρ[∂tv+(v⋅∇)v]=−∇p+η∇2v+f,∇⋅v=0.\rho\big[\partial_t\mathbf v+(\mathbf v\cdot\nabla)\mathbf v\big]=-\nabla p+\eta\nabla^2\mathbf v+\mathbf f,\qquad \nabla\cdot\mathbf v=0.ρ[∂t​v+(v⋅∇)v]=−∇p+η∇2v+f,∇⋅v=0.

Here f\mathbf ff is force per volume. The advective term (v⋅∇)v(\mathbf v\cdot\nabla)\mathbf v(v⋅∇)v accounts for acceleration as fluid moves into a region of different velocity. The viscous term follows from the constitutive relation between stress and velocity gradients. Conservation fixes the balance equation; it does not fix the numerical viscosity. In the incompressible problem, pressure also enforces the constraint ∇⋅v=0\nabla\cdot\mathbf v=0∇⋅v=0.

The same equations describe chemically different liquids once their coefficients and boundary conditions are supplied. Molecular confinement or driving faster than local relaxation can remove the required separation of scales. Slowly relaxing composition or orientation must be added as extra fields in mixtures or liquid crystals. Even with few fields, nonlinear advection can generate complex vortices and turbulence. The reduction is in the information needed to specify the dynamics, not necessarily in the difficulty of solving it.

References
  • Feynman, Leighton and Sands, The Feynman Lectures on Physics, II Ch. 40. Continuity, material acceleration, and incompressible flow.
  • Feynman, Leighton and Sands, The Feynman Lectures on Physics, II §41–2. Viscous stress and the Newtonian momentum equation.

Chapter 2

Collective order and its limits

Interactions can select an arrangement that persists over distances far larger than the particle spacing. Crystals organize positions, ferromagnets align magnetic moments, and antiferromagnets alternate them. An order parameter is an observable chosen to distinguish these arrangements: the average that detects one kind of order can miss another completely.

This chapter develops that choice of observable and the physics it reveals. Liquid crystals retain directional order while flowing; phase separation organizes composition. Near a continuous transition, growing correlations lead to critical scaling, whose common features can be explained by the renormalization group. The last examples extend the picture: broken continuous symmetries produce soft modes, vortex binding distinguishes the two sides of a BKT transition, and glasses develop rigidity when structural relaxation becomes too slow to observe. These forms of organization have different thermodynamic and dynamical origins.

11Crystallization: free energy and nucleation

Cooling a liquid can produce a repeating density pattern with a definite orientation. The atomic positions are selected collectively: translating a free crystal as a whole leaves its energy unchanged, while displacing one atom relative to its neighbors generally costs energy.

For NNN particles at positions rj\mathbf r_jrj​, the static structure factor at scattering wavevector q\mathbf qq detects positional correlations:

S(q)=1N⟨∣∑j=1Neiq⋅rj∣2⟩.S(\mathbf q)=\frac1N\left\langle\left|\sum_{j=1}^{N}e^{i\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf r_j}\right|^2\right\rangle.S(q)=N1​⟨​j=1∑N​eiq⋅rj​​2⟩.

At reciprocal-lattice vectors, which match the crystal periodicity, amplitudes from many particles add coherently. The resulting Bragg peaks distinguish long-range periodic order from the short-range correlations of an ordinary liquid.

At fixed temperature and pressure, equilibrium favors the phase with lower Gibbs free energy G=E+pV−TSG=E+ pV-TSG=E+pV−TS. Interaction energy and entropy both matter. Alder and Wainwright's hard-sphere simulations provided a particularly clear example: particles that only exclude overlap can crystallize without any attraction. At high density, an ordered arrangement can allow enough additional particle motion to outweigh the entropy lost by selecting lattice positions. A regular-looking snapshot can therefore belong to the phase with greater total entropy at fixed volume and energy.

Thermodynamic preference does not guarantee immediate crystallization. In a simple nucleation approximation, a spherical crystal region in a metastable liquid has

ΔG(R)=4πR2γ−4π3R3Δg,\Delta G(R)=4\pi R^2\gamma-\frac{4\pi}{3}R^3\Delta g,ΔG(R)=4πR2γ−34π​R3Δg,

where γ>0\gamma>0γ>0 is interfacial tension and Δg>0\Delta g>0Δg>0 the bulk free-energy advantage per volume. The barrier peaks at R=2γ/ΔgR=2\gamma/\Delta gR=2γ/Δg: smaller nuclei tend to shrink, while larger ones can grow. Impurities, interfacial anisotropy, and cooling rate alter this route. They help determine whether the sample crystallizes and which defects remain, even when its equilibrium phase is already known.

References
  • Alder and Wainwright (1957), Phase Transition for a Hard Sphere System. Hard-sphere crystallization without attractive interactions.
  • Feynman, Leighton and Sands, The Feynman Lectures on Physics, II Ch. 30. Crystal periodicity, reciprocal lattices, and defects.

12Ferromagnetism and spontaneous symmetry breaking

A ferromagnetic domain retains a collective orientation without a continuing applied field. The Ising model isolates one mechanism by assigning a spin si=±1s_i=\pm1si​=±1 to each of NNN lattice sites, representing a moment constrained to one axis:

H=−J∑⟨ij⟩sisj−h∑isi,m=1N∑i⟨si⟩.H=-J\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}s_is_j-h\sum_i s_i,\qquad m=\frac1N\sum_i\langle s_i\rangle.H=−J⟨ij⟩∑​si​sj​−hi∑​si​,m=N1​i∑​⟨si​⟩.

The first sum runs over neighbors, J>0J>0J>0 favors parallel spins, and hhh is field energy per spin. At h=0h=0h=0, reversing all spins leaves HHH unchanged. An ordered state with a selected sign of magnetization mmm breaks this symmetry: its orientation is not shared by every state with the same energy.

Flipping a region inside an ordered state creates a domain wall of unfavorable neighbor pairs. Ordering depends on the competition between the wall's energy and the number of ways walls can occur. Replacing each neighbor by its mean gives m=tanh⁡[(zJm+h)/(kBT)]m=\tanh[(zJm+h)/(k_BT)]m=tanh[(zJm+h)/(kB​T)], where zzz is the coordination number. This mean-field approximation predicts a transition but misses spatial fluctuations. The nearest-neighbor chain has no ordered phase at nonzero temperature, whereas Onsager's exact square-lattice solution establishes a finite-temperature transition. Dimensionality changes the balance between excitation cost and entropy.

For a finite zero-field system, an equilibrium average over both orientations gives m=0m=0m=0. Spontaneous magnetization is defined by taking the thermodynamic limit before removing an infinitesimal selecting field. Long-range spin correlations also reveal the order.

Real ferromagnets add exchange anisotropy and long-range magnetic fields. Forming oppositely magnetized domains can reduce the external field energy, leaving little net sample moment. Distinguishing such a sample from a disordered magnet therefore requires spatial correlations or domain-sensitive measurements, not only the total magnetization.

13Antiferromagnetism and staggered order

Regularly alternating magnetic moments can have zero net magnetization. On a bipartite lattice, divided into sublattices AAA and BBB with every nearest-neighbor bond joining unlike sublattices, the alternating pattern is detected by comparing their moments.

For spin operators Si\mathbf S_iSi​, the antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model is H=J∑⟨ij⟩Si⋅SjH=J\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\mathbf S_i\cdot\mathbf S_jH=J∑⟨ij⟩​Si​⋅Sj​, with J>0J>0J>0. For NNN sites divided equally between the sublattices, define

M=1N∑i⟨Si⟩,L=1N∑iηi⟨Si⟩,\mathbf M=\frac1N\sum_i\langle\mathbf S_i\rangle,\qquad \mathbf L=\frac1N\sum_i\eta_i\langle\mathbf S_i\rangle,M=N1​i∑​⟨Si​⟩,L=N1​i∑​ηi​⟨Si​⟩,

where ηi=+1\eta_i=+1ηi​=+1 on AAA and −1-1−1 on BBB. The uniform magnetization M\mathbf MM may vanish while the staggered magnetization L\mathbf LL remains nonzero. This is Néel order. Magnetic diffraction detects it at wavevectors matching the alternation, even when a magnetometer records almost no total moment.

One microscopic origin of the exchange is the half-filled, one-orbital Hubbard model. Electrons hop with amplitude ttt and pay energy UUU for double occupancy. For U≫tU\gg tU≫t, real charge transfer is costly, but virtual hopping through doubly occupied intermediate states lowers the energy of antiparallel configurations. Second-order perturbation theory gives J≃4t2/UJ\simeq4t^2/UJ≃4t2/U. Charge motion can therefore be suppressed while spins still interact on a much smaller energy scale. Magnons are quantized collective oscillations of the ordered spins.

The lattice and symmetry determine whether Néel order survives. A triangle cannot make all three neighboring classical moments antiparallel; this incompatibility is frustration. Strong quantum fluctuations can also prevent order. At nonzero temperature, an isotropic two-dimensional model with short-range exchange has no conventional magnetic long-range order; anisotropy or interlayer coupling can allow real layered materials to order. The relevant observable must follow the spatial organization favored by these interactions.

References
  • Néel (1970), Nobel Lecture. Opposite sublattice magnetizations and antiferromagnetic ordering.
  • Hubbard (1963), Electron correlations in narrow energy bands. The on-site interaction model whose half-filled strong-coupling limit generates exchange.

14Nematic liquid crystals: alignment without a lattice

A nematic liquid crystal flows while retaining a preferred molecular axis. Its molecules continually change neighbors, but their orientations remain correlated. This distinguishes orientational order from the repeating positional order of a crystal.

For rods whose two ends are equivalent, n\mathbf nn and −n-\mathbf n−n describe the same axis. A vector average can therefore vanish in an aligned sample. In three dimensions, the appropriate order parameter is the tensor

Qij=⟨uiuj−δij3⟩,Q_{ij}=\left\langle u_i u_j-\frac{\delta_{ij}}3\right\rangle,Qij​=⟨ui​uj​−3δij​​⟩,

where u\mathbf uu is a molecular unit axis. An isotropic distribution has Q=0Q=0Q=0. For a uniaxial nematic, Qij=S(ninj−δij/3)Q_{ij}=S(n_i n_j-\delta_{ij}/3)Qij​=S(ni​nj​−δij​/3), where n\mathbf nn is the director, an unoriented axis, and SSS measures alignment. This form respects the head–tail symmetry.

Alignment need not be caused by attractive forces. In Onsager's model of long rigid hard rods, nearly perpendicular rods exclude more volume from one another than nearly parallel rods. At sufficient concentration, losing orientational entropy can release enough positional freedom to lower the total free energy. The model makes an entropic origin of directional order explicit, much as hard spheres demonstrate an entropic route to crystallization.

Spatial variations of the director cost elastic free energy. Splay makes neighboring axes diverge, twist rotates the director between neighboring planes, and bend curves its direction along itself. Boundaries and electric fields can select the director and thereby control the optical response. Defects occur where the surrounding orientation pattern cannot be continued smoothly through a core without reducing the order. The tensor and these deformation costs provide a continuum description of an orientationally ordered fluid; polar or layered liquid-crystal phases require additional variables.

References
  • Onsager (1949), The Effects of Shape on the Interaction of Colloidal Particles. Excluded-volume ordering in the slender, rigid hard-rod limit.
  • MIT, Electromagnetic Energy: Liquid Crystal Display Technology, Lecture 26. Directional optical response and electric-field control of liquid-crystal orientation.
  • University of Michigan, Lecture 7: Excluded Volume. Excluded volume and the self-consistent orientational distribution of hard rods.

15Phase separation and spinodal instability

A binary mixture can prefer two different compositions to one uniform composition. Whether separation starts from small fluctuations or requires a finite nucleus depends on the local stability of the initial mixture.

Let c(r)c(\mathbf r)c(r) be the local fraction of one component. A minimal free energy is

F[c]=∫[f(c)+κ2∣∇c∣2]dV,F[c]=\int\left[f(c)+\frac\kappa2|\nabla c|^2\right]dV,F[c]=∫[f(c)+2κ​∣∇c∣2]dV,

where fff is bulk free-energy density and κ>0\kappa>0κ>0 penalizes composition gradients. Cahn and Hilliard's gradient construction represents an interface as a smooth composition profile with a free-energy cost. The variational derivative μ=δF/δc=f′(c)−κ∇2c\mu=\delta F/\delta c=f'(c)-\kappa\nabla^2cμ=δF/δc=f′(c)−κ∇2c has units of energy per volume for this dimensionless choice of ccc; it is proportional to the chemical-potential difference per particle.

With constant mobility M>0M>0M>0 and flux j=−M∇μ\mathbf j=-M\nabla\muj=−M∇μ, composition conservation gives the Cahn–Hilliard equation ∂tc=M∇2μ\partial_tc=M\nabla^2\mu∂t​c=M∇2μ. A Fourier perturbation about uniform c0c_0c0​ has growth rate

λ(k)=−Mk2[f′′(c0)+κk2].\lambda(k)=-Mk^2[f''(c_0)+\kappa k^2].λ(k)=−Mk2[f′′(c0​)+κk2].

When f′′(c0)<0f''(c_0)<0f′′(c0​)<0, a small enrichment lowers local free energy and attracts further material. Long-wavelength fluctuations grow, while the gradient penalty stabilizes short wavelengths. This is spinodal decomposition. For closed boundaries with no flux and the corresponding natural boundary condition on ccc, or for periodic boundaries, the dynamics conserves mean composition and satisfies dF/dt=−M∫∣∇μ∣2dV≤0dF/dt=-M\int|\nabla\mu|^2dV\leq0dF/dt=−M∫∣∇μ∣2dV≤0.

The initial wavelength need not be the final domain size: domains usually coarsen as interfacial area decreases. Outside the spinodal region, f′′(c0)>0f''(c_0)>0f′′(c0​)>0 can stabilize small perturbations even though a two-phase state has lower free energy. Separation then requires nucleation across a barrier. Flow, elastic stress, reactions, or long-range interactions can modify either process and can arrest coarsening.

References
  • Cahn and Hilliard (1958), Free Energy of a Nonuniform System. I. Interfacial Free Energy. Gradient free energy of nonuniform mixtures and interfacial cost; the dynamics and stability calculation are developed here.

16Criticality and growing correlations

Near a liquid–gas critical point, density fluctuations can scatter visible light and make the fluid cloudy. Their growth reflects the weakening of the restoring force against long-wavelength density changes. At a conventional continuous transition, the correlation length diverges in the ideal infinite equilibrium system.

For a scalar order parameter ϕ\phiϕ, the connected correlation function at separation rrr is G(r)=⟨ϕ(r)ϕ(0)⟩−⟨ϕ⟩2G(r)=\langle\phi(\mathbf r)\phi(0)\rangle-\langle\phi\rangle^2G(r)=⟨ϕ(r)ϕ(0)⟩−⟨ϕ⟩2. Subtracting the mean isolates fluctuations. Away from criticality, GGG typically decays exponentially beyond a correlation length ξ\xiξ. Near a short-range critical point,

ξ∼∣t∣−ν,G(r)∼r−(d−2+η)(a≪r≪ξ).\xi\sim|t|^{-\nu},\qquad G(r)\sim r^{-(d-2+\eta)}\quad(a\ll r\ll\xi).ξ∼∣t∣−ν,G(r)∼r−(d−2+η)(a≪r≪ξ).

Here t=(T−Tc)/Tct=(T-T_c)/T_ct=(T−Tc​)/Tc​, ddd is dimension, aaa a microscopic length, and ν,η\nu,\etaν,η critical exponents. A widening interval between aaa and ξ\xiξ admits approximately scale-free correlations.

A Gaussian free energy illustrates the softening:

F=12∫[r0ϕ2+κ∣∇ϕ∣2]dV.F=\frac12\int[r_0\phi^2+\kappa|\nabla\phi|^2]dV.F=21​∫[r0​ϕ2+κ∣∇ϕ∣2]dV.

For r0,κ>0r_0,\kappa>0r0​,κ>0, a Fourier mode has variance proportional to kBT/(r0+κk2)k_BT/(r_0+\kappa k^2)kB​T/(r0​+κk2). As r0r_0r0​ decreases, long waves become inexpensive and ξ=κ/r0\xi=\sqrt{\kappa/r_0}ξ=κ/r0​​ grows. Interactions between fluctuations, omitted here, change the critical exponents in many physical systems.

Response grows with the correlated region: a small conjugate field can change many degrees of freedom together. Relaxation also commonly slows as those regions reorganize. Finite size and finite observation time cut off this growth and round thermodynamic singularities. Establishing a critical description therefore requires consistent scaling of correlations and response as a control parameter approaches the transition; a fitted power law in one observable supplies only part of that evidence.

  • Tong, Statistical Field Theory, §3.2.1. Scaling relations and interacting critical exponents.

17Universality and the renormalization group

A fluid near its liquid–gas endpoint and a uniaxial magnet can share critical exponents despite different constituents and forces. Universality concerns specified long-distance observables after material-dependent units and amplitudes have been accounted for.

The renormalization group averages over short-distance fluctuations and rescales lengths. Effective coupling constants change under this operation. A fixed point is an effective description reproduced by the transformation. Wilson's explanation of universality is that different microscopic models can approach the same fixed point and therefore acquire the same critical scaling.

Near a fixed point, a small coupling perturbation ggg transforms to leading order as

g′≃byg,g'\simeq b^y g,g′≃byg,

with length rescaling factor b>1b>1b>1. A relevant perturbation has y>0y>0y>0 and grows; an irrelevant one has y<0y<0y<0 and diminishes. For y=0y=0y=0, the perturbation is marginal, and nonlinear terms in its evolution must be examined. Temperature distance from criticality is usually relevant, explaining why the transition must be approached by tuning. Many details of short-range interactions are irrelevant, explaining why their differences do not change leading exponents.

Spatial dimension, order-parameter symmetry, interaction range, disorder, and additional soft fields help determine the accessible fixed points. A scalar liquid–gas endpoint can have static Ising critical behavior after the appropriate thermodynamic variables are identified. Its dynamics need not match a magnet's: a conserved density relaxes differently from a nonconserved magnetization.

Experiments also have a finite range of lengths and temperatures. A weak perturbation that is relevant may grow appreciably only at very large scales, producing crossover between apparent scaling regimes. Predicting universality therefore requires both identifying a fixed point and checking which physically allowed perturbations destabilize it.

References
  • Wilson (1982), The Renormalization Group and Critical Phenomena, Nobel Lecture. Renormalization-group explanation of universality and critical scaling.
  • Tong, Statistical Field Theory, §3. Fixed points and relevant, irrelevant, and marginal perturbations.

18Goldstone modes and the cost of a slow twist

An ordered phase may select an orientation even though its Hamiltonian favors none. Uniformly rotating that state then costs no energy. Neighboring regions rotated by different amounts do cost energy, but their mismatch becomes arbitrarily small when the variation is spread over a long wavelength. Goldstone modes are the resulting gapless collective excitations of a broken continuous global symmetry.

For an angular coordinate θ(r)\theta(\mathbf r)θ(r), invariance under uniform shifts excludes a local restoring term proportional to θ2\theta^2θ2. With stiffness KKK, the leading static cost is instead

F[θ]=K2∫∣∇θ∣2dV.F[\theta]=\frac K2\int|\nabla\theta|^2dV.F[θ]=2K​∫∣∇θ∣2dV.

A sinusoidal distortion has energy density proportional to Kk2Kk^2Kk2 times its squared amplitude, where kkk is wave number. Introducing an inertial coefficient χ\chiχ, the Lagrangian density L=χ(∂tθ)2/2−K∣∇θ∣2/2\mathcal L=\chi(\partial_t\theta)^2/2-K|\nabla\theta|^2/2L=χ(∂t​θ)2/2−K∣∇θ∣2/2 gives frequency ω=K/χ∣k∣\omega=\sqrt{K/\chi}|k|ω=K/χ​∣k∣. Its quantum excitation energy vanishes as k→0k\to0k→0.

Symmetry constrains the soft coordinate, but the dynamics determines the dispersion. An isotropic ferromagnet has a quadratic long-wavelength magnon dispersion rather than this linear one. In nonrelativistic systems, two broken generators can act as conjugate variables of a single mode; Watanabe and Murayama's counting result makes this distinction precise. Broken crystal rotations likewise need not add independent modes beyond those already described by displacement fields.

A weak anisotropy or selecting field adds a cost for uniform rotation and can open a gap. Long-range forces and dynamical gauge fields modify the elementary argument as well. The existence of the ordered state must also be checked: thermal fluctuations can destroy continuous-symmetry order in low dimensions. Within these conditions, the long-wavelength spectrum follows from the symmetries and dynamics of the collective coordinate.

References
  • Watanabe and Murayama (2012), Unified Description of Nambu-Goldstone Bosons without Lorentz Invariance. Nonrelativistic Goldstone counting, conjugate pairs of generators, and dispersion relations.
  • Watanabe and Murayama (2013), Redundancies in Nambu-Goldstone Bosons. Redundant broken spatial symmetries and the absence of additional rotational phonons.

19Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless transition: unbinding vortices

Planar spins in an infinite two-dimensional system with short-range isotropic interactions cannot sustain ordinary magnetization at nonzero temperature. Long-wavelength angular fluctuations destroy it. A sharp transition can nevertheless distinguish bound vortex pairs from free vortices.

A vortex has integer winding qqq: the spin angle changes by 2πq2\pi q2πq around a loop enclosing its core. Smooth deformations preserve that integer until a core crosses the loop or the angular field becomes undefined. With phase stiffness ρs\rho_sρs​, the long-distance free energy is F=(ρs/2)∫∣∇θ∣2d2rF=(\rho_s/2)\int|\nabla\theta|^2d^2rF=(ρs​/2)∫∣∇θ∣2d2r. A unit vortex has ∣∇θ∣=1/r|\nabla\theta|=1/r∣∇θ∣=1/r outside core radius aaa, hence

Ev≃πρsln⁡(L/a)+Ecore.E_v\simeq\pi\rho_s\ln(L/a)+E_{\rm core}.Ev​≃πρs​ln(L/a)+Ecore​.

The system size is LLL and EcoreE_{\rm core}Ecore​ is the core energy. Approximately (L/a)2(L/a)^2(L/a)2 possible vortex positions provide entropy 2kBln⁡(L/a)2k_B\ln(L/a)2kB​ln(L/a). Energy and positional entropy therefore compete at the same logarithmic order.

Below the Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless transition, opposite vortices remain paired. Spin correlations decay algebraically because smooth fluctuations persist; this is quasi-long-range order. Above the transition, unbound vortices produce exponential decay. The single-vortex estimate identifies the competition, while the effect of vortex pairs must be included in the effective long-distance stiffness. Just below the transition it obeys

ρs(Tc−)=2kBTcπ,\rho_s(T_c^-)=\frac{2k_BT_c}{\pi},ρs​(Tc−​)=π2kB​Tc​​,

the universal jump predicted by Nelson and Kosterlitz in this stiffness normalization.

The same reasoning applies to appropriate two-dimensional neutral superfluids. Finite size cuts off the logarithms, while interlayer coupling, anisotropy, or electromagnetic screening can change the transition. Measurements of vortex separation, correlations, and stiffness test different parts of the mechanism. The topology here is the winding of a classical field, distinct from intrinsic topological order in a quantum many-body state.

References
  • Kosterlitz and Thouless (1973), Ordering, metastability and phase transitions in two-dimensional systems. Vortex binding and the two-dimensional transition mechanism.
  • Nelson and Kosterlitz (1977), Universal Jump in the Superfluid Density of Two-Dimensional Superfluids. Universal jump of the renormalized superfluid stiffness.

20Glasses and the slowing of structural relaxation

A glass resists shear without the repeating atomic pattern of a crystal. Cooling a liquid while avoiding crystallization can make its structural relaxation time τα\tau_\alphaτα​ exceed the experiment's duration. Rearrangements that would relax a liquid's stress then occur too slowly for the sample to flow appreciably.

The operational glass transition occurs when τα(T)\tau_\alpha(T)τα​(T) becomes comparable with a preparation or observation time. Its measured temperature therefore depends on cooling rate. Once out of equilibrium, the material can age: its properties continue changing with elapsed time after preparation. Neither finite-time arrest nor aging alone identifies an equilibrium thermodynamic singularity.

Relaxation is spatially heterogeneous. A particle can be confined by its neighbors, and escape may require several neighbors to move. To quantify this, let wi(t)=1w_i(t)=1wi​(t)=1 if particle iii moves less than a specified microscopic distance during time ttt, and zero otherwise. For NNN particles, define Q(t)=N−1∑iwi(t)Q(t)=N^{-1}\sum_iw_i(t)Q(t)=N−1∑i​wi​(t) and

χ4(t)=N[⟨Q(t)2⟩−⟨Q(t)⟩2].\chi_4(t)=N\big[\langle Q(t)^2\rangle-\langle Q(t)\rangle^2\big].χ4​(t)=N[⟨Q(t)2⟩−⟨Q(t)⟩2].

Expanding the variance expresses χ4\chi_4χ4​ as a sum of correlations between local mobilities. Independently rearranging particles contribute only local fluctuations; groups moving together add correlated contributions. Its normalization and interpretation depend on the ensemble and displacement threshold, so it is not automatically a unique correlation volume.

Competing theories explain growing barriers through structural organization, cooperative rearrangements, or dynamical facilitation, in which a mobile region enables nearby motion. Kinetically constrained models show explicitly how restricted moves can generate slow heterogeneous dynamics despite simple equilibrium statistics. Distinguishing these explanations requires more than fitting the average relaxation time: spatial mobility correlations and responses to changed preparation provide additional tests. An ideal equilibrium glass transition remains a separate theoretical question from the established observation of kinetic arrest.

References
  • Berthier et al. (2005), Direct experimental evidence of a growing length scale accompanying the glass transition. Experimental dynamical susceptibilities and evidence for a growing scale of correlated relaxation.
  • Garrahan and Chandler (2002), Geometrical explanation and scaling of dynamical heterogeneities in glass forming systems. Heterogeneous relaxation in kinetically constrained facilitation models.

Chapter 3

Quantum matter makes new excitations

The effective particles in matter need not coincide with its microscopic constituents. A phonon is a quantum of coordinated atomic motion. A Fermi-liquid quasiparticle carries electronic charge but has a dispersion and lifetime modified by the surrounding electrons. A fractional quantum Hall quasihole has charge and exchange statistics that emerge from the correlated many-electron state.

The chapter follows these excitations and the states that support them. Bose condensation describes macroscopic occupation of an orbital, while superfluidity and superconductivity concern phase stiffness and response. Mott insulation and Anderson localization suppress transport through interactions and coherent disorder scattering, respectively. Intrinsic topological order and topological bands then show two different ways in which quantum states carry structure beyond an ordinary local order parameter. In each case, identifying the excitation or response is the first step toward determining the low-energy description and its range of validity.

21Fermi liquids and long-lived quasiparticles

Many metals behave at low temperature like electron gases with altered masses and interactions, even when microscopic repulsion is substantial. Landau's Fermi-liquid theory describes their low-energy excitations as quasiparticles: particles dressed by the response of the surrounding electrons, with a sufficiently narrow energy width to remain identifiable.

A Fermi surface separates occupied and unoccupied momentum states at zero temperature in a noninteracting gas. In a Fermi liquid, a corresponding surface survives. For volume VVV, quasiparticle energy ϵp∗\epsilon^*_{\mathbf p}ϵp∗​, and residual interaction fpp′f_{\mathbf p\mathbf p'}fpp′​, the energy change due to small occupation changes δnp\delta n_{\mathbf p}δnp​ can be expanded as

δE=∑pϵp∗δnp+12V∑p,p′fpp′δnpδnp′.\delta E=\sum_{\mathbf p}\epsilon^*_{\mathbf p}\delta n_{\mathbf p}+\frac{1}{2V}\sum_{\mathbf p,\mathbf p'}f_{\mathbf p\mathbf p'}\delta n_{\mathbf p}\delta n_{\mathbf p'}.δE=p∑​ϵp∗​δnp​+2V1​p,p′∑​fpp′​δnp​δnp′​.

Spin labels are suppressed. A quasiparticle retains the electron's charge and, in a spin-rotation-invariant setting, its spin quantum number. Its velocity differs from the bare value. The interaction term also modifies compressibility and magnetic susceptibility, so replacing the electron mass alone is insufficient.

Pauli exclusion blocks most final scattering states near the Fermi surface. In a conventional three-dimensional Fermi liquid, the quasiparticle energy width behaves as Γ∝ϵ2+(πkBT)2\Gamma\propto\epsilon^2+(\pi k_BT)^2Γ∝ϵ2+(πkB​T)2, where ϵ\epsilonϵ is measured from the chemical potential. At zero temperature, Γ/∣ϵ∣→0\Gamma/|\epsilon|\to0Γ/∣ϵ∣→0 as ϵ→0\epsilon\to0ϵ→0: lower-energy excitations become better defined. The same description gives a heat capacity linear in temperature, with coefficient set by the quasiparticle density of states.

This low-energy organization can fail in one dimension, at some quantum critical points, or when another phase intervenes. Spectral line widths and thermodynamic responses must therefore agree with the quasiparticle picture. A fitted effective mass by itself does not establish that the corresponding excitation is long lived.

22Phonons: quantized lattice vibrations

A neutron can scatter from a crystal and transfer a definite energy without adding or removing an atom. It can instead create a phonon, one quantum of a collective vibrational mode.

For a periodic chain of atoms with mass MMM, spacing aaa, displacement uju_juj​, momentum pjp_jpj​, and nearest-neighbor spring constant κ\kappaκ, the harmonic Hamiltonian and mode frequency ωk\omega_kωk​ at wave number kkk are

H=∑j[pj22M+κ2(uj+1−uj)2],ωk=2κM∣sin⁡ka2∣.H=\sum_j\left[\frac{p_j^2}{2M}+\frac\kappa2(u_{j+1}-u_j)^2\right],\qquad \omega_k=2\sqrt{\frac\kappa M}\left|\sin\frac{ka}{2}\right|.H=j∑​[2Mpj2​​+2κ​(uj+1​−uj​)2],ωk​=2Mκ​​​sin2ka​​.

The normal modes labeled by kkk are coordinated patterns that oscillate independently. Transforming to these coordinates makes HHH a sum of harmonic oscillators, with energies ℏωk(nk+1/2)\hbar\omega_k(n_k+1/2)ℏωk​(nk​+1/2). Increasing integer nkn_knk​ by one adds a phonon.

A mode extends through the crystal, but superposing nearby wave numbers produces a wave packet that propagates at group velocity dωk/dkd\omega_k/dkdωk​/dk. No atom travels with it across the sample. A one-phonon state has zero mean displacement; its energy appears in displacement and momentum fluctuations. A classical lattice wave is instead represented by a coherent superposition of occupation numbers with an oscillating mean displacement. Quantizing a collective coordinate therefore introduces distinct quantum states of the same atomic motion.

At small ∣k∣a|k|a∣k∣a, ωk≃aκ/M∣k∣\omega_k\simeq a\sqrt{\kappa/M}|k|ωk​≃aκ/M​∣k∣, recovering continuum sound. Anharmonicity allows phonons to interact and decay. A particle description remains useful when a mode's width is small relative to its frequency. Crystal momentum ℏk\hbar kℏk is defined modulo a reciprocal-lattice momentum and is not generally the sample's total mechanical momentum. Long-lived modes provide a compact account of energy transport and scattering without requiring the motion of every atom to be tracked.

23Bose–Einstein condensation and macroscopic occupation

Bose–Einstein condensation is macroscopic occupation of a one-particle orbital. More precisely, trace out all but one particle and normalize the resulting one-particle density matrix to trace NNN, the total particle number. Its matrix elements describe single-particle coherence between positions, and its eigenvalues are orbital occupations that sum to NNN. Condensation occurs when one eigenvalue is proportional to NNN. For a uniform ideal gas this state is the zero-momentum orbital. The macroscopic occupation describes a many-particle state; it does not bind the particles into one object.

For noninteracting bosons of mass mmm, the occupation of a level of energy ϵ\epsilonϵ is [e(ϵ−μ)/(kBT)−1]−1[e^{(\epsilon-\mu)/(k_BT)}-1]^{-1}[e(ϵ−μ)/(kB​T)−1]−1. Taking the lowest energy as zero, the chemical potential μ\muμ approaches zero from below as the gas is cooled. In three dimensions, the excited states can then hold at most

nex=ζ(3/2)λT3,λT=2πℏ2mkBT.n_{\rm ex}=\frac{\zeta(3/2)}{\lambda_T^3},\qquad \lambda_T=\sqrt{\frac{2\pi\hbar^2}{mk_BT}}.nex​=λT3​ζ(3/2)​,λT​=mkB​T2πℏ2​​.

Here nexn_{\rm ex}nex​ is excited-state number density, λT\lambda_TλT​ the thermal wavelength, and ζ(3/2)=∑j=1∞j−3/2\zeta(3/2)=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}j^{-3/2}ζ(3/2)=∑j=1∞​j−3/2. At total density nnn, the transition satisfies nλT3=ζ(3/2)n\lambda_T^3=\zeta(3/2)nλT3​=ζ(3/2). Below this temperature TcT_cTc​, particles exceeding the thermal capacity occupy the ground state. Writing the ground-state population as N0N_0N0​, the condensate fraction is N0/N=1−(T/Tc)3/2N_0/N=1-(T/T_c)^{3/2}N0​/N=1−(T/Tc​)3/2.

This saturation mechanism requires Bose statistics but no attraction. Collisions are nevertheless important for equilibrating experimental gases. Penrose and Onsager's density-matrix criterion extends the definition to interacting or nonuniform systems: an eigenvalue of order NNN identifies condensation, and its eigenfunction identifies the occupied orbital. That orbital need not be a plane wave.

The first dilute rubidium experiments observed a narrow component whose population grew on cooling. Trap geometry changes the available excited states, so the uniform-gas formulas do not apply unchanged. A uniform ideal gas in one or two dimensions has no finite-temperature condensation in the thermodynamic limit. Condensation also differs from superfluidity: occupation is a property of the state, whereas persistent flow depends on its response and accessible excitations.

References

24Superfluidity: excitations and persistent flow

A fluid current decays by transferring energy and momentum to other degrees of freedom. Superfluid flow can persist because the excitation spectrum and the possible changes of its collective phase restrict those decay processes.

For a homogeneous fluid moving past a weak obstacle, an excitation of momentum p\mathbf pp and rest-frame energy ϵ(p)\epsilon(\mathbf p)ϵ(p) has energy balance ϵ(p)−v⋅p\epsilon(\mathbf p)-\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf pϵ(p)−v⋅p. Emission cannot lower the energy if this remains positive. For an isotropic spectrum, Landau's criterion is

v<vL,vL=min⁡p>0ϵ(p)p.v<v_L,\qquad v_L=\min_{p>0}\frac{\epsilon(p)}p.v<vL​,vL​=p>0min​pϵ(p)​.

This tests a specified excitation channel, rather than proving stability against every possible disturbance.

For a dilute Bose gas of particles of mass mmm, with repulsive contact coupling ggg and number density nnn, Bogoliubov theory gives ϵ(p)=[p2/(2m)][p2/(2m)+2gn]\epsilon(p)=\sqrt{[p^2/(2m)][p^2/(2m)+2gn]}ϵ(p)=[p2/(2m)][p2/(2m)+2gn]​. At low momentum it becomes cpcpcp, with c=gn/mc=\sqrt{gn/m}c=gn/m​, and this spectrum gives vL=cv_L=cvL​=c. The ideal gas has quadratic excitations and zero Landau threshold. Condensation alone has therefore not supplied this energetic obstruction to decay.

Phase stiffness is the free-energy cost of a spatial variation in the collective phase θ\thetaθ. For a neutral condensate, vs=(ℏ/m)∇θ\mathbf v_s=(\hbar/m)\nabla\thetavs​=(ℏ/m)∇θ. Single-valuedness quantizes circulation around a loop avoiding vortex cores in units of h/mh/mh/m. Changing the winding requires the phase to become undefined somewhere along the process, for example when a vortex crosses the flowing channel. Such a phase slip connects states that cannot be joined by a small smooth phase deformation.

Boundaries, obstacles, and thermal fluctuations can enable vortex nucleation at velocities below the elementary-excitation estimate. Different channels can thus have different critical velocities for the same fluid. The superfluid fraction measured by flow or rotational response also need not equal the condensate fraction: phase rigidity, occupation, and metastability are related but distinct properties.

25Superconductivity and electromagnetic phase stiffness

A superconductor exhibits the Meissner effect: in an appropriate equilibrium regime, magnetic field is expelled from its bulk. This response distinguishes it from a hypothetical perfect conductor, which would preserve previously trapped flux when its resistance vanished.

In conventional superconductors, lattice vibrations can mediate an effective attraction between electrons near the Fermi surface. The Bardeen–Cooper–Schrieffer state coherently combines many overlapping Cooper pairs. For isotropic pairing, let ξk\xi_{\mathbf k}ξk​ be normal-state energy relative to the chemical potential and Δ\DeltaΔ the gap. The fermionic excitation energies are

Ek=ξk2+∣Δ∣2,E_{\mathbf k}=\sqrt{\xi_{\mathbf k}^2+|\Delta|^2},Ek​=ξk2​+∣Δ∣2​,

Pairing changes the excitation spectrum, while phase stiffness determines the long-wavelength current response.

Write an effective pair field as Ψ=npeiθ\Psi=\sqrt{n_p}e^{i\theta}Ψ=np​​eiθ. With pair charge qp=−2eq_p=-2eqp​=−2e, its gauge-invariant momentum is ℏ∇θ−qpA\hbar\nabla\theta-q_p\mathbf Aℏ∇θ−qp​A. For effective pair mass mpm_pmp​, a local continuum model with a positive quadratic cost for this momentum gives

j=npqpmp(ℏ∇θ−qpA).\mathbf j=\frac{n_pq_p}{m_p}(\hbar\nabla\theta-q_p\mathbf A).j=mp​np​qp​​(ℏ∇θ−qp​A).

The ratio np/mpn_p/m_pnp​/mp​ parametrizes superfluid stiffness; in a material it need not be obtained by simply counting microscopic pairs. Taking a curl in a vortex-free region gives ∇×j=−(npqp2/mp)B\nabla\times\mathbf j=-(n_pq_p^2/m_p)\mathbf B∇×j=−(np​qp2​/mp​)B. Maxwell's equations then imply exponential field penetration with length λ=mp/(μ0npqp2)\lambda=\sqrt{m_p/(\mu_0n_pq_p^2)}λ=mp​/(μ0​np​qp2​)​ in SI units, where μ0\mu_0μ0​ is the vacuum permeability. The phase depends on gauge, but this magnetic response does not.

Type-II superconductors can admit quantized flux vortices, whose motion dissipates energy. Strong current, temperature, or field can also destroy the superconducting response. Unconventional superconductors may have gap nodes and pairing mechanisms different from lattice-mediated attraction. The common macroscopic feature is electromagnetic phase stiffness; the isotropic BCS construction supplies one microscopic realization.

  • Bardeen, Cooper and Schrieffer (1957), Theory of Superconductivity. Microscopic pairing theory and the excitation gap of conventional superconductors.

26Mott insulation and the separation of charge and spin scales

A partially filled noninteracting band normally permits conduction. Strong interactions can instead make charge transfer costly and produce a Mott insulator. The one-orbital Hubbard model isolates this competition:

H=−t∑⟨ij⟩,σ(ciσ†cjσ+h.c.)+U∑ini↑ni↓.H=-t\sum_{\langle ij\rangle,\sigma}(c^\dagger_{i\sigma}c_{j\sigma}+\mathrm{h.c.})+U\sum_i n_{i\uparrow}n_{i\downarrow}.H=−t⟨ij⟩,σ∑​(ciσ†​cjσ​+h.c.)+Ui∑​ni↑​ni↓​.

Here ciσ†c^\dagger_{i\sigma}ciσ†​ creates an electron of spin σ\sigmaσ at site iii, ciσc_{i\sigma}ciσ​ removes one, and niσ=ciσ†ciσn_{i\sigma}=c^\dagger_{i\sigma}c_{i\sigma}niσ​=ciσ†​ciσ​ is the number operator. The parameters ttt and U>0U>0U>0 are nearest-neighbor hopping energy and the cost of double occupancy. The Hermitian conjugate supplies reverse hopping. At one electron per site, hopping tends to create a doubly occupied site and an empty site. It gains kinetic energy but costs interaction energy.

In the atomic limit t=0t=0t=0, the cost is explicit. When UUU is large compared with the bandwidth, the range of noninteracting band energies, finite hopping need not restore mobile charge. A useful diagnostic is the charge gap

Δc=E0(N+1)+E0(N−1)−2E0(N),\Delta_c=E_0(N+1)+E_0(N-1)-2E_0(N),Δc​=E0​(N+1)+E0​(N−1)−2E0​(N),

where E0(N)E_0(N)E0​(N) is the ground-state energy with NNN electrons. A positive gap in the thermodynamic limit separates particle-addition and particle-removal thresholds. Meanwhile, virtual hopping generates spin exchange of order 4t2/U4t^2/U4t2/U. Low-energy spin excitations can remain active far below the charge-transfer scale.

The effective low-energy variables are then local moments rather than freely moving electrons. Magnetic order may accompany this state, but the strong-coupling charge gap and an ordering-induced band gap have different origins. Filling matters as much as interaction strength: the same argument does not guarantee insulation away from integer occupancy. Additional orbitals and lattice motion complicate real materials. Ultracold bosons in optical lattices offer a separate realization in which repulsion suppresses number fluctuations at integer filling, with different particle statistics but the same basic competition between hopping and interaction energy.

References
  • Hubbard (1963), Electron correlations in narrow energy bands. On-site electronic correlations and the competition between atomic and band limits.
  • Greiner et al. (2002), Quantum phase transition from a superfluid to a Mott insulator in a gas of ultracold atoms. Interaction-driven Mott transition of bosonic atoms in an optical lattice.

27Anderson localization by coherent scattering

Random scattering can slow a classical random walk, but a coherent wave can cease spreading altogether. Interference among repeated scattering paths produces Anderson localization even without classical barriers enclosing each localized state.

For a one-dimensional lattice, the stationary amplitude ψj\psi_jψj​ obeys

Eψj=−t(ψj+1+ψj−1)+Vjψj.E\psi_j=-t(\psi_{j+1}+\psi_{j-1})+V_j\psi_j.Eψj​=−t(ψj+1​+ψj−1​)+Vj​ψj​.

The hopping energy is ttt and the static on-site energies VjV_jVj​ are independent random variables. Without disorder, eigenstates are extended waves. For generic uncorrelated disorder in this model, eigenstates are exponentially localized, with envelope ∣ψj∣∼e−∣j−j0∣a/ξ|\psi_j|\sim e^{-|j-j_0|a/\xi}∣ψj​∣∼e−∣j−j0​∣a/ξ. Here j0j_0j0​ is a localization center, aaa the lattice spacing, and ξ\xiξ the localization length. Weak disorder can make ξ\xiξ much larger than an experimental sample.

A wave packet is a superposition of eigenstates. When the participating states are localized, their evolving phases do not produce ordinary indefinite diffusion. Replacing every scattering amplitude by an independent probability would discard the interference responsible for this result. In three dimensions, localized and extended states can occur at different energies, separated by a mobility edge. The dimensional and symmetry assumptions therefore belong to the localization prediction.

Saturated wave-packet expansion and exponentially suppressed transmission are useful signatures, provided absorption and finite-time trapping are distinguished from coherent localization. Absorption removes wave intensity; localization redistributes a conserved wave into spatially confined states. Inelastic scattering, time-dependent disorder, or interactions can restore transport by opening additional processes. Localization of an interacting many-body system is a separate question. The single-particle result already shows how a wave interacting with many scattering sites can acquire a collective transport length without requiring many occupied particles.

References
  • Anderson (1958), Absence of Diffusion in Certain Random Lattices. Suppression of quantum diffusion by static disorder.
  • Abrahams et al. (1979), Scaling Theory of Localization: Absence of Quantum Diffusion in Two Dimensions. Dimensional scaling of coherent noninteracting disordered transport.

28Fractional charge and anyonic statistics

A two-dimensional electron fluid can support a localized excitation of charge +e/3+e/3+e/3, although every electron has charge −e-e−e. The excitation is a deficit spread across a correlated many-electron state. Fractionalization assigns new quantum numbers to that collective excitation without subdividing an electron.

Laughlin's state at filling ν=1/m\nu=1/mν=1/m, with odd integer m≥3m\geq3m≥3, makes the construction explicit. Filling is the ratio of electron number to the degeneracy of a Landau level, a quantized cyclotron-energy level. With zj=xj+iyjz_j=x_j+iy_jzj​=xj​+iyj​ and magnetic length ℓB=ℏ/(e∣B∣)\ell_B=\sqrt{\hbar/(e|B|)}ℓB​=ℏ/(e∣B∣)​, a suitable field convention gives

Ψm∝∏i<j(zi−zj)mexp⁡ ⁣[−∑i∣zi∣24ℓB2].\Psi_m\propto\prod_{i<j}(z_i-z_j)^m\exp\!\left[-\sum_i\frac{|z_i|^2}{4\ell_B^2}\right].Ψm​∝i<j∏​(zi​−zj​)mexp[−i∑​4ℓB2​∣zi​∣2​].

The zeros suppress close electron pairs and reduce repulsive interaction energy. Multiplying by ∏i(zi−η)\prod_i(z_i-\eta)∏i​(zi​−η) creates a quasihole near η\etaη. In the screened Laughlin-fluid regime, its integrated electron deficit carries charge +e/m+e/m+e/m. The electron number is unchanged; compensating charge lies elsewhere, for example at the droplet edge.

Arovas, Schrieffer, and Wilczek evaluated the geometric phase of slowly moving quasiholes. After subtracting ordinary electromagnetic and dynamical phases, taking one quasihole fully around another contributes statistical phase of magnitude 2π/m2\pi/m2π/m. An exchange has magnitude π/m\pi/mπ/m, with sign set by orientation and field convention. These are Abelian anyons: exchanges act by commuting scalar phases, rather than the bosonic or fermionic exchange signs of the constituents.

The calculation requires a gapped correlated bulk and well-separated quasiholes moved slowly enough to avoid other excitations. The wavefunction is exact for special interactions and approximates a phase realized more generally. Interferometry at ν=1/3\nu=1/3ν=1/3 has observed phase slips consistent with the predicted full-winding phase, in devices designed to suppress charging effects. Charge, spatial profile, and interference thus provide distinct tests of the emergent excitation.

References
  • Laughlin (1983), Anomalous Quantum Hall Effect: An Incompressible Quantum Fluid with Fractionally Charged Excitations. Laughlin trial state and fractionally charged quasiholes.
  • Arovas, Schrieffer and Wilczek (1984), Fractional Statistics and the Quantum Hall Effect. Geometric-phase calculation of quasihole charge and fractional statistics.
  • Nakamura et al. (2020), Direct observation of anyonic braiding statistics. Interference phase slips consistent with a full-winding anyonic phase at filling 1/3.

29Intrinsic topological order in the toric code

Different quantum ground states can agree on every local measurement while differing in observables that wind around the whole system. Kitaev's toric code gives an exactly solvable example of intrinsic topological order, with both nonlocal state structure and fractionalized excitations.

Place a spin-1/21/21/2 on every edge of a square lattice with periodic boundaries in both directions. This gives a torus, with Hamiltonian

H=−Je∑sAs−Jm∑pBp.H=-J_e\sum_s A_s-J_m\sum_p B_p.H=−Je​s∑​As​−Jm​p∑​Bp​.

The operator AsA_sAs​ is the product of Pauli XXX operators on edges meeting vertex sss; BpB_pBp​ is the product of Pauli ZZZ operators around plaquette ppp, an elementary square. They commute because a vertex and plaquette share either zero or two edges. Positive Je,JmJ_e,J_mJe​,Jm​ favor As=Bp=+1A_s=B_p=+1As​=Bp​=+1.

These local constraints leave four ground states on the torus. Operators in a small contractible region cannot distinguish them, while loops winding around the two independent torus directions can. A string of Pauli ZZZ operations creates vertex violations at its endpoints; a dual-lattice string of Pauli XXX operations creates plaquette violations. Separating either pair costs no additional energy. Taking an electric-type endpoint around a magnetic-type endpoint multiplies the state by −1-1−1. These labels refer to two kinds of constraint violation, not physical electric and magnetic charges.

Weak local perturbations that preserve the bulk gap generally split the ground states by an amount exponentially small in system size. Changing a nonlocal state label requires an operation extending around the system, which accounts for this suppression. Thermal errors are different: a pair of excitations can be created and then separate without a growing energy barrier. For weak local coupling to a thermal bath, the two-dimensional toric code does not become a stable passive quantum memory merely by increasing its size at fixed nonzero temperature.

This intrinsic order differs from the topology of an ordinary band insulator. Its ground-state degeneracy and mutual anyonic statistics belong to the correlated many-body state and cannot be captured by a conventional local order parameter.

References
  • Kitaev (2003; preprint 1997), Fault-tolerant quantum computation by anyons. Commuting lattice constraints, topological ground-state degeneracy, and anyonic excitations.
  • Castelnovo and Chamon (2007), Entanglement and topological entropy of the toric code at finite temperature. Finite-temperature topological entropy and the order of the temperature and system-size limits.
  • Alicki, Fannes, and Horodecki (2009), On thermalization in Kitaev's 2D model. System-size-independent upper bound on relaxation time for weak local coupling to a thermal reservoir.

30Topological bands and protected boundaries

An insulating bulk can constrain its boundary to carry electronic states. To distinguish this from accidental surface conduction, we need a bulk property that cannot change continuously while the relevant gap and symmetries remain intact.

For a two-dimensional noninteracting band insulator, the occupied Bloch states define a geometry over crystal momentum. Berry curvature Ωn(k)\Omega_n(\mathbf k)Ωn​(k) measures the geometric phase of band nnn around an infinitesimal momentum-space loop. Its integral over the Brillouin zone gives the total Chern number:

C=12π∑n occupied∫BZΩn(k) d2k,σxy=Ce2h.C=\frac1{2\pi}\sum_{n\,\mathrm{occupied}}\int_{\rm BZ}\Omega_n(\mathbf k)\,d^2k,\qquad \sigma_{xy}=C\frac{e^2}{h}.C=2π1​noccupied∑​∫BZ​Ωn​(k)d2k,σxy​=Che2​.

The integer CCC cannot change under a smooth deformation that keeps occupied and empty bands separated. Here σxy\sigma_{xy}σxy​ is zero-temperature Hall conductivity, eee is the elementary charge, and hhh is Planck's constant; the sign follows the chosen orientation. Haldane's model demonstrates that a nonzero CCC is possible with zero net magnetic flux per unit cell.

Across an interface, the difference in Chern numbers fixes the net number of boundary branches moving in one direction minus those moving oppositely. This is bulk–boundary correspondence. An edge with an unpaired directed branch is chiral: static disorder has no reverse-moving partner into which that branch can scatter at the same edge. The statement constrains boundary propagation, while contacts and other channels still affect measured resistance.

Protection can also rely on symmetry. A quantum spin Hall insulator has counterpropagating edge partners related by time reversal. For a single pair, time-reversal-preserving single-particle disorder cannot elastically backscatter one partner into the other. Magnetic perturbations, coupling opposite edges, and suitable interaction processes can change that conclusion. Mercury-telluride quantum wells provide experimental evidence for this boundary conduction. Unlike intrinsic topological order, this band structure requires neither fractionalized charge nor topological ground-state degeneracy on a torus.

References
  • Haldane (1988), Model for a Quantum Hall Effect without Landau Levels. Chern-insulating lattice model with zero net magnetic flux per unit cell.
  • Kane and Mele (2005), Z2 Topological Order and the Quantum Spin Hall Effect. Time-reversal-invariant band topology and quantum spin Hall edge states.
  • König et al. (2007), Quantum Spin Hall Insulator State in HgTe Quantum Wells. Transport evidence for quantum spin Hall boundaries in HgTe wells.

Chapter 4

Rhythms, patterns, and failure

A fluid heated from below can change from conducting heat without moving to transporting it through circulating rolls. The molecular interactions remain the same; a collective state loses stability. Identifying a reference state and calculating which disturbances grow provides one route to understanding pattern formation.

Other organized behavior requires different tools. Coupling can synchronize existing oscillators, chemical reactions can generate a stable rhythm, and dispersion can balance nonlinear wave steepening to preserve a pulse. Turbulence is described through transfer between scales, while avalanches and fracture follow the propagation of local instabilities. Jamming makes the contact geometry itself central to rigidity. Throughout these examples, the useful quantities are measurable features of the dynamics: growth rates, frequencies, wavelengths, energy fluxes, and mechanical response. Similar-looking patterns can arise from different mechanisms, so the explanation must connect those observables to the interactions that produce them.

31Synchronization of coupled oscillators

Oscillators with different natural frequencies can acquire a common frequency through coupling. Each oscillator repeatedly traverses a cycle, and its phase records progress around that cycle. Frequency locking permits a fixed phase offset; it does not require identical instantaneous states.

In the Kuramoto model, NNN oscillators have phases θi\theta_iθi​, natural angular frequencies ωi\omega_iωi​, and coupling strength KKK:

θ˙i=ωi+KN∑j=1Nsin⁡(θj−θi).\dot\theta_i=\omega_i+\frac{K}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\sin(\theta_j-\theta_i).θ˙i​=ωi​+NK​j=1∑N​sin(θj​−θi​).

Define the collective phase ψ\psiψ and alignment magnitude rrr by reiψ=N−1∑jeiθjre^{i\psi}=N^{-1}\sum_j e^{i\theta_j}reiψ=N−1∑j​eiθj​. The coupling term becomes Krsin⁡(ψ−θi)Kr\sin(\psi-\theta_i)Krsin(ψ−θi​): relative to the collective phase, it speeds a lagging oscillator and slows one that is ahead. If the group rotates at frequency Ω\OmegaΩ, a locked oscillator satisfies ωi−Ω=Krsin⁡(θi−ψ)\omega_i-\Omega=Kr\sin(\theta_i-\psi)ωi​−Ω=Krsin(θi​−ψ). Locking is possible only when its frequency mismatch is at most KrKrKr.

This relation explains the feedback behind collective onset. Alignment increases rrr, strengthening the effective coupling and allowing more oscillators to lock. For suitable frequency distributions and sufficiently strong coupling, a synchronized subset persists in the large-population limit. The threshold and its character depend on that distribution and the coupling structure.

A phase-only description assumes that amplitude disturbances relax quickly compared with changes in timing. Strong coupling, delays, noise, or sparse connections can invalidate this reduction. Experimentally, stable phase differences and a response to altered coupling provide stronger evidence for mutual synchronization than a shared frequency alone. A common external driver can entrain otherwise uncoupled oscillators, so its influence must be separated from interactions among the units.

32Chemical oscillations and delayed inhibition

A reacting mixture can repeatedly change color while its fuel is steadily consumed. The concentrations that oscillate are intermediates: substances produced by one reaction step and removed by another. A catalyst can cycle between forms differing by electron transfer; their different colors make the oscillation visible while the catalyst is regenerated overall.

The Belousov–Zhabotinsky reaction couples rapid amplification to slower recovery. In the Oregonator, Field and Noyes reduced its chemical mechanism to a few intermediates. Autocatalysis allows one intermediate to accelerate its own production. A competing process restores an inhibitor that suppresses this growth. After the activated intermediate is depleted and inhibition relaxes, the cycle can begin again.

For an activating concentration xxx and a slower inhibitory concentration yyy, write x˙=f(x,y)\dot x=f(x,y)x˙=f(x,y) and y˙=g(x,y)\dot y=g(x,y)y˙​=g(x,y), where fff and ggg are net production rates. Positive feedback initially raises xxx; delayed inhibition turns the increase around. Nonlinear reaction rates can make the resulting trajectory approach an attracting limit cycle, a closed orbit to which nearby states return. The cycle's stability explains why concentrations can recover their rhythm after a small perturbation. Feedback signs alone do not ensure that such an orbit exists; its existence and period must follow from the rate equations.

Maintaining the cycle consumes free energy. A sealed batch can oscillate transiently while its reactants are depleted, often with a changing period. A flow reactor can replenish reagents and remove products to sustain an approximately stationary rhythm. The oscillating intermediate concentrations therefore coexist with a directed chemical conversion. Measuring that conversion, the feedback reactions, and the recovery time connects the visible rhythm to its mechanism.

References
  • Field and Noyes (1974), Oscillations in chemical systems. IV. Limit cycle behavior in a model of a real chemical reaction. Oregonator reaction mechanism and attracting concentration cycles.
