33Turing patterns from diffusion-driven instability

Diffusion smooths each concentration field, yet can destabilize a mixture of reacting substances. The key is that unequal transport rates change the feedback between the fields. A uniform state stabilized by local reactions may then become unstable to spatial disturbances.

For concentrations uuu and vvv, let fff and ggg be net local reaction rates, and Du,Dv>0D_u,D_v>0Du​,Dv​>0 their diffusivities:

∂tu=f(u,v)+Du∇2u,∂tv=g(u,v)+Dv∇2v.\partial_tu=f(u,v)+D_u\nabla^2u,\qquad \partial_tv=g(u,v)+D_v\nabla^2v.∂t​u=f(u,v)+Du​∇2u,∂t​v=g(u,v)+Dv​∇2v.

At a uniform steady state, the reaction Jacobian JJJ is the matrix of first derivatives of fff and ggg. Assume its eigenvalues have negative real parts, so a spatially uniform disturbance decays. A Fourier disturbance with wave number qqq instead evolves under J−q2diag⁡(Du,Dv)J-q^2\operatorname{diag}(D_u,D_v)J−q2diag(Du​,Dv​). If the diffusivities were equal, diffusion would simply shift both eigenvalues left and improve stability. Unequal diffusivities can instead make one eigenvalue positive over a band of nonzero qqq.

Turing's construction thus converts a local stability problem into a wavelength-dependent one. Local activation and more rapidly spreading inhibition provide an intuitive realization. The fastest-growing wave number sets an initial spacing; nonlinear reactions then determine whether growth saturates into spots, stripes, or another state. Boundaries restrict the allowed wavelengths, so chemistry alone does not select the final pattern.

The calculation establishes a possible mechanism for spatial organization. Applying it to a tissue requires identifying the relevant interacting substances, their transport, and the instability of the uniform state. Cell migration, mechanical stresses, or pre-existing signals can generate similar appearances. The decisive evidence is how the pattern responds when those reaction and transport processes are changed.

34Convection and the instability of a heated layer

In a fluid heated from below, an upward-displaced parcel can remain warmer and less dense than its surroundings. Buoyancy then strengthens the displacement. Viscosity damps the motion and thermal diffusion erases the temperature difference; convection begins when buoyant feedback overcomes them.

For layer depth HHH, imposed temperature difference ΔT\Delta TΔT, expansion coefficient α\alphaα, gravitational acceleration ggg, kinematic viscosity ν\nuν, and thermal diffusivity κ\kappaκ, the dimensionless Rayleigh number is

Ra=gαΔTH3νκ.\mathrm{Ra}=\frac{g\alpha\Delta T H^3}{\nu\kappa}.Ra=νκgαΔTH3​.

Increasing depth strongly favors instability through the factor H3H^3H3. In the Boussinesq approximation, density variations are retained in buoyancy but neglected elsewhere, allowing an incompressible velocity description. Linearizing the coupled temperature and velocity equations about the motionless conducting state gives growth rates for disturbances. Their first crossing through zero sets a critical Rayleigh number that depends on the mechanical and thermal boundary conditions.

Near onset, an unstable mode can saturate into rolls: warm fluid rises, cooler fluid descends, and circulation carries additional heat. Its amplitude and spacing describe a coordinated flow of many molecules. The layer depth supplies a natural length for the rolls, while the boundary conditions and geometry select among the allowed modes. Heat flux and the response to a changed temperature difference test the predicted onset and subsequent growth.

The imposed temperature difference maintains this organization. Several flow patterns can coexist or compete, with imperfections and preparation selecting the observed one. Stronger forcing can destabilize a steady pattern into time dependence and turbulence. A stability calculation explains the onset, while the nonlinear fluid dynamics determines what follows it.

35Deterministic chaos and finite prediction horizons

A deterministic equation can specify a unique trajectory while nearby trajectories rapidly separate. Finite uncertainty in the initial state then limits how far ahead the motion can be predicted, even without random forcing.

Lorenz illustrated this with a truncated convection model. Its variables x,y,zx,y,zx,y,z are rescaled amplitudes of circulation and temperature patterns, and σ,r,b\sigma,r,bσ,r,b are dimensionless parameters:

x˙=σ(y−x),y˙=rx−y−xz,z˙=xy−bz.\dot x=\sigma(y-x),\qquad \dot y=rx-y-xz,\qquad \dot z=xy-bz.x˙=σ(y−x),y˙​=rx−y−xz,z˙=xy−bz.

In chaotic regimes, trajectories remain bounded without approaching a repeating cycle. An initially small separation δ(0)\delta(0)δ(0) can grow as δ(t)∼δ(0)eλt\delta(t)\sim\delta(0)e^{\lambda t}δ(t)∼δ(0)eλt while it remains small. A positive largest Lyapunov exponent λ\lambdaλ measures the average rate of exponential separation. Stretching amplifies differences, while the nonlinear dynamics repeatedly returns trajectories to a bounded region.

For acceptable forecast error Δ\DeltaΔ, this growth gives an approximate horizon tpred≃λ−1ln⁡[Δ/δ(0)]t_{\rm pred}\simeq\lambda^{-1}\ln[\Delta/\delta(0)]tpred​≃λ−1ln[Δ/δ(0)]. Improving initial precision by a fixed factor adds a fixed amount of useful forecast time. It does not proportionally extend the horizon. Eventually the error reaches the scale of the explored region and exponential growth saturates.

Long-term distributions and correlations can remain predictable after a particular trajectory becomes uncertain. Those statistical properties are associated with an attractor, the set approached by trajectories from a range of initial conditions. Irregular data alone do not establish chaos: stochastic forcing and measurement noise can also generate irregularity. Evidence requires dynamical sensitivity assessed with finite-record and numerical errors under control. The distinction is between predicting a specific evolving state and predicting the statistical behavior of the same deterministic system.

References
  • Lorenz (1963), Deterministic nonperiodic flow. Bounded nonperiodic motion and sensitivity to initial conditions in a convection truncation.

36Solitons and the balance of nonlinearity with dispersion

A localized wave packet usually spreads because its Fourier components propagate differently. In some nonlinear media, amplitude-dependent propagation counteracts that dispersion and produces a persistent pulse. The moving object is a field profile, not a fixed set of material particles.

For a rescaled amplitude u(x,t)u(x,t)u(x,t), the dimensionless Korteweg–de Vries equation is

∂tu+6u∂xu+∂x3u=0.\partial_tu+6u\partial_xu+\partial_x^3u=0.∂t​u+6u∂x​u+∂x3​u=0.

The nonlinear term makes larger amplitudes propagate faster and tends to steepen a wave. The third derivative produces dispersion. Their balance admits a pulse of speed c>0c>0c>0 and initial center x0x_0x0​:

u(x,t)=c2sech⁡2[c2(x−ct−x0)].u(x,t)=\frac c2\operatorname{sech}^2\left[\frac{\sqrt c}{2}(x-ct-x_0)\right].u(x,t)=2c​sech2[2c​​(x−ct−x0​)].

Its height is c/2c/2c/2 and its width scales as c−1/2c^{-1/2}c−1/2. These properties are linked by the equation; arbitrary heights, widths, and speeds cannot be combined into a persistent solution.

A solitary wave is a localized traveling profile. The stronger soliton property includes collisions: solutions containing several pulses show that they recover their shapes and speeds afterward, with shifted positions. The collision changes where a pulse is found but preserves the relation between its shape and speed. Zabusky and Kruskal's numerical study identified this persistence and showed why the pulses could be treated as effective objects.

Physical water channels, optical fibers, and plasmas add losses, forcing, higher-order dispersion, and other modes. A long-lived pulse may closely approximate a soliton over a useful distance while gradually radiating or changing shape. Comparing pulses before and after a collision, including any emitted waves and position shifts, tests the stronger claim more directly than observing one isolated pulse travel.

References
  • Zabusky and Kruskal (1965), Interaction of “Solitons” in a Collisionless Plasma and the Recurrence of Initial States. Persistent Korteweg–de Vries pulses and their collision behavior.

Back to contents ↑

37Turbulence and transfer between scales

Stirring a fluid at a large scale can produce motion across a wide range of smaller scales. Individual eddies continually change, but the average transfer of kinetic energy can be reproducible. Turbulence is therefore often described through correlations and fluxes between scales rather than a single flow trajectory.

In three-dimensional incompressible turbulence, nonlinear advection transfers energy toward small scales where viscosity dissipates it. At sufficiently large Reynolds number, the ratio of inertial to viscous effects, an inertial range can separate forcing from dissipation. Neither directly dominates the energy balance within that range.

Let ε\varepsilonε be the mean energy transfer rate per unit mass and δuℓ\delta u_\ellδuℓ​ a typical velocity difference across separation ℓ\ellℓ. Kolmogorov's similarity argument assumes sufficiently homogeneous and locally isotropic statistics and uses only ε\varepsilonε and ℓ\ellℓ to estimate

δuℓ∼(εℓ)1/3.\delta u_\ell\sim(\varepsilon\ell)^{1/3}.δuℓ​∼(εℓ)1/3.

The corresponding energy spectrum scales as E(k)∼ε2/3k−5/3E(k)\sim\varepsilon^{2/3}k^{-5/3}E(k)∼ε2/3k−5/3, where kkk is wave number and ∫E(k) dk\int E(k)\,dk∫E(k)dk is kinetic energy per unit mass. The mean flux through the inertial range is approximately independent of scale.

This cascade is a statistical balance: individual transfers fluctuate and can run in either direction. Intermittency describes the uneven concentration of strong velocity gradients and dissipation in space and time. It modifies some scaling predictions and the tails of probability distributions beyond the simplest similarity picture.

Two-dimensional, rotating, stratified, or wall-bounded flows have additional constraints that change energy transfer. A short spectral interval near k−5/3k^{-5/3}k−5/3 is consequently insufficient to establish the full cascade picture. Flux measurements, scale separation, and tests of anisotropy connect the observed spectrum to the mechanism assumed in the estimate.

References
  • Kolmogorov (1941), The local structure of turbulence in incompressible viscous fluid for very large Reynolds numbers. Similarity hypotheses for high-Reynolds-number locally isotropic turbulence.

Back to contents ↑

38Avalanches and the propagation of local instability

Slow loading can produce sudden bursts because one local rearrangement changes the forces on neighboring regions. A slip or spin reversal may push another region past its threshold, which triggers further changes. An avalanche is a connected sequence of such events, distinguishable from the next sequence when loading is slow compared with its duration.

In a simple branching approximation, each rearrangement triggers a mean number of successors. If this number is below one, events usually die out quickly. Near one, many generations can occur and large bursts become possible. Real materials add spatial correlations, force balance, and interactions that may stabilize some neighbors while destabilizing others. These details determine whether the branching picture is useful and which event statistics follow.

Driven magnetic reversal gives a concrete example. The zero-temperature random-field Ising model assigns different local biases to spins; slowly changing the external field initiates avalanches of spin flips. Sethna and colleagues showed a disorder-controlled critical point separating regimes with and without a macroscopic magnetization jump. Slow driving separates the events, but disorder must also be appropriately tuned to reach this critical behavior.

Event sizes, durations, and shapes can be measured as field, disorder, and sample size change. Finite-size scaling, the systematic dependence of distributions on system dimensions, tests a collective description more strongly than a power-law fit over a short interval. At higher driving rates, independent events can overlap and appear to be a single large burst. Other models contain feedback that maintains proximity to an instability, but this is an additional mechanism, not a consequence of slow loading alone. Identifying how a rearrangement transmits force and how the sequence stops is essential to comparing different crackling systems.

References
  • Sethna, Dahmen, and Myers (2001), Crackling noise. Scaling of intermittent collective responses in crackling systems.
  • Sethna et al. (1993), Hysteresis and hierarchies: Dynamics of disorder-driven first-order phase transformations. Disorder-controlled avalanches and a critical magnetization jump in the driven random-field Ising model.

Back to contents ↑

39Jamming and contact constraints

Compressing disordered particles can make them resist shear without forming a crystal or permanent bonds. Their contacts constrain motions that would otherwise let them rearrange. Jamming concerns the onset of mechanical rigidity in this contact network.

Consider frictionless spheres with finite-range repulsion at zero temperature. The packing fraction ϕ\phiϕ measures the fraction of space occupied. At low enough density, energy minimization removes overlaps and leaves particles unconstrained. Compression eventually produces a load-bearing contact structure. Above the jamming threshold, small shear deformations cost energy, giving a shear modulus, the linear ratio of shear stress to strain.

Constraint counting provides a first estimate. In ddd dimensions, NNN particle centers have approximately dNdNdN translational degrees of freedom. Each independent frictionless contact supplies one normal constraint. If zzz is the mean number of contacts per particle, the number of contacts is Nz/2Nz/2Nz/2, suggesting z≃2dz\simeq2dz≃2d at marginal rigidity. Global motions and particles that are not constrained by the network must be treated separately. Geometry, redundant constraints, and force balance also matter; a contact count alone does not prove rigidity.

Near the threshold, collective modes with very small restoring forces allow unusually easy distortions. O'Hern and colleagues' simulations connected this excess of low-frequency modes with the onset of pressure and elastic response in disordered sphere packings. The threshold is defined for a specified particle model and preparation protocol, rather than being a universal density for all granular matter.

Friction, particle shape, attraction, and loading history change the available constraints. A stable arch in a funnel also relies on boundaries absent from a periodic packing. The contact network and its mechanical response, not crowding alone, determine whether a disordered assembly is rigid.

References
  • O’Hern, Silbert, Liu, and Nagel (2003), Jamming at zero temperature and zero applied stress: The epitome of disorder. Jamming thresholds, contact counting, elastic response, and low-frequency modes in frictionless repulsive packings.

Back to contents ↑

40Fracture and the energy released by a crack

A scratch can make glass fail under a load that an otherwise similar specimen withstands. The crack concentrates stress near its tip and changes the elastic field throughout a much larger region. Extending it releases stored mechanical energy while breaking bonds and creating surfaces.

Griffith's energetic criterion compares these two changes. The energy-release rate GGG is the reduction in the appropriate mechanical potential energy per added projected crack area, including the effect of the loading apparatus. Crack advance becomes energetically possible when GGG reaches the fracture resistance GcG_cGc​. For an ideally brittle material, GcG_cGc​ is the cost of the two newly created surfaces. Real fracture resistance can also include plastic deformation and other dissipation near the tip.

For an isolated crack of half-length aaa in a large elastic plate under tensile stress σ\sigmaσ, Young's modulus EEE sets the stiffness scale. The energy-release rate behaves as

G∼σ2aE,G\sim\frac{\sigma^2a}{E},G∼Eσ2a​,

with geometry and plane-stress or plane-strain conditions determining additional factors. A longer crack therefore reaches a fixed resistance at a smaller applied stress. The flaw's influence extends far beyond the bonds at its tip because the surrounding solid relaxes as it grows.

Reaching GcG_cGc​ does not by itself determine whether growth is stable. The change of G−GcG-G_cG−Gc​ with crack extension depends on specimen geometry, material resistance, and whether the apparatus holds force or displacement fixed. Crack motion also emits stress waves and may branch or encounter regions of different toughness; fatigue introduces further history dependence. The useful collective variables are the advancing crack and its surrounding elastic field, which connect local separation to the load-bearing capacity of the whole specimen.

References
  • Griffith (1921), The phenomena of rupture and flow in solids. Energetic criterion for brittle fracture and the dependence of strength on flaw size.

Chapter 5

Living matter: structures that maintain and reproduce themselves

Living systems combine several kinds of persistence. A membrane retains its shape while its molecules move; a gene circuit maintains a concentration pattern while proteins are replaced; a reproducing group passes its organization to descendants. Each calls for a different explanation. We begin with molecular structures and then add feedback, chemical energy, and reproduction.

The first examples connect familiar statistical mechanics to biology: membrane assembly, polymer elasticity, and protein folding. Reaction networks then introduce amplification, memory, and timing. The final entries examine how chemical signals specify position, how cells compensate for disturbances, and how groups of cells acquire a shared life cycle. Throughout, the useful large-scale variables are things we can measure—curvature, extension, concentration, period, or reproductive output. Explaining their behavior gives us concrete pieces of biological organization without requiring a single mechanism to explain life as a whole.

41Molecular self-assembly: Membranes from molecular interactions

Many membrane lipids have a head group that interacts favorably with water and hydrocarbon tails whose exposure to water is unfavorable. Such molecules are called amphiphiles. In water they can aggregate with their tails sheltered inside: a micelle has a small hydrophobic interior, a bilayer contains two opposing molecular layers, and a vesicle is a closed bilayer surrounding water. Simple lipid mixtures form these structures without cellular machinery.

Assembly depends on the free energy of the entire mixture. Sheltering the tails competes with the loss of translational entropy as freely dispersed molecules enter aggregates. Head groups need space, and connected tails must fill the interior without excessive stretching. These packing constraints help determine whether an aggregate favors strong curvature or an almost flat surface. The theory of Israelachvili, Mitchell, and Ninham connects molecular geometry and interaction free energies to this choice of structure.

At equilibrium, molecules exchange between aggregates and solution until their chemical potentials agree. Over an aggregation range, adding amphiphile mainly increases the amount in aggregates, while the free-molecule concentration changes much less. Molecular species, temperature, salt, and concentration determine which structures are stable. A bilayer can close into a vesicle because removing an exposed edge can outweigh the bending cost of closure.

Once a membrane exists, we can describe its bending stiffness, surface tension, and permeability without tracking every lipid. These properties belong to the extended assembly. Cellular membranes use this physical foundation, but also contain proteins and actively maintain differences between their two sides. Equilibrium assembly explains how a boundary can form; transport and chemical reactions explain how a living cell maintains and uses it.

References
  • Israelachvili, Mitchell & Ninham (1976), Theory of self-assembly of hydrocarbon amphiphiles into micelles and bilayers. Connects aggregate free energies and molecular packing constraints to the formation of micelles and bilayers.
  • Alberts et al. (2002), The Chemical Components of a Cell. Explains amphiphilic cell components and the noncovalent interactions underlying molecular assembly.

Back to contents ↑

42Polymer elasticity: A molecular chain becomes an entropic spring

A polymer is a molecule made from many connected units. A long chain can resist extension even when its chemical bonds barely stretch: there are many more coiled configurations than extended ones. Holding its ends far apart reduces the number of accessible configurations and therefore raises its free energy. DNA, which stores hereditary sequence information, provides a measurable example of this entropic elasticity.

Replace the molecule by NNN independently oriented segments of length bbb, where bbb is an effective segment length. For the end-to-end vector R\mathbf RR, the random-walk result is ⟨R2⟩=Nb2\langle R^2\rangle=Nb^2⟨R2⟩=Nb2. At large NNN and R≪NbR\ll NbR≪Nb, its probability density is Gaussian. Constraining the vector to R\mathbf RR therefore costs F(R)−F(0)≃3kBTR2/(2Nb2)F(\mathbf R)-F(\mathbf0)\simeq3k_BT R^2/(2Nb^2)F(R)−F(0)≃3kB​TR2/(2Nb2), and the applied force is f≃3kBTR/(Nb2)\mathbf f\simeq3k_BT\mathbf R/(Nb^2)f≃3kB​TR/(Nb2). Here kBk_BkB​ is Boltzmann's constant and TTT is absolute temperature. The vector constraint matters: the probability density of the distance alone also includes the spherical measure 4πR24\pi R^24πR2.

Real DNA retains orientational correlations over a persistence length. The wormlike-chain model represents this local stiffness by a bending-energy cost. Its use in DNA stretching studies explains why an ideal random walk works only after averaging over enough contour length. Close to full extension, the Gaussian spring law fails because the finite contour length becomes important; at still larger forces, stretching the molecular backbone also matters.

The collective behavior here occurs within one molecule, among its many internal degrees of freedom. Its effective spring constant measures the configurations removed by an imposed deformation. This also explains the factor of TTT: for a fixed ideal-chain geometry, heating strengthens the entropic restoring force.

References
  • Bustamante et al. (1994), Entropic elasticity of lambda-phage DNA. Discusses the entropic elasticity of stretched DNA; the ideal-chain derivation in this entry is an illustrative statistical-mechanical calculation.
  • Marko & Siggia (1995), Stretching DNA. Develops the wormlike-chain description of DNA stretching, including bending stiffness and thermal fluctuations.

Back to contents ↑

43Protein folding: A sequence forms a reproducible structure

A protein is a chain of amino acids, molecular building blocks with chemically different side groups. The sequence fixes the order of these groups, while their interactions with one another and with the surrounding water favor some chain shapes over others. Many proteins repeatedly occupy a relatively narrow family of three-dimensional structures. Those structures arrange binding surfaces or bring chemical groups together to accelerate reactions, a process called catalysis.

A conformation is one spatial arrangement of the chain. We can describe folding through a free-energy landscape over conformations: nonpolar groups tend to become buried, and hydrogen bonds and other interactions favor particular local arrangements. The native state is the structural ensemble associated with the folded protein under specified conditions. Thermal motion continues within it. Refolding experiments showed that some isolated proteins recover their active structure in a suitable solution, demonstrating that the sequence and environment can be sufficient to specify this ensemble.

In a two-state approximation, collect conformations into folded and unfolded ensembles with free energies GFG_FGF​ and GUG_UGU​. Their equilibrium probabilities obey PF/PU=exp⁡[−(GF−GU)/(kBT)]P_F/P_U=\exp[-(G_F-G_U)/(k_BT)]PF​/PU​=exp[−(GF​−GU​)/(kB​T)]. A favorable folded free energy determines occupancy, while barriers on the landscape determine how quickly folding occurs. A chain can instead become trapped or aggregate with other chains. Molecular chaperones are proteins that assist folding or prevent aggregation; many consume ATP, a molecule whose chemical conversion supplies free energy.

The reduction to a few structural states makes binding and mechanical response tractable despite the enormous configuration space. It works differently for different proteins: some remain broadly disordered, and others acquire structure when they bind a partner. A structure prediction addresses which configurations are favored; explaining folding also requires the routes, rates, and cellular conditions that make them accessible.

References
  • Alberts et al. (2002), The Shape and Structure of Proteins. Explains protein sequence, stabilizing interactions, structural ensembles, and the role of molecular chaperones.
  • Cooper (2000), Protein Folding and Processing. Describes spontaneous refolding in solution and folding assistance within cells.
  • Weinreb et al. (1996), NACP, a protein implicated in Alzheimer’s disease and learning, is natively unfolded. Reports conformational measurements showing that the studied protein occupies a disordered ensemble under the tested solution conditions.

Back to contents ↑

44Autocatalysis: Chemistry that accelerates its own production

A catalyst accelerates a reaction without being consumed overall in that reaction. When a product catalyzes further production of itself, its concentration affects its own growth rate: this is autocatalysis. The feedback can also run through several species, each helping produce another. Catalysis changes reaction rates; the free energy and material needed for net production still come from the supplied reactants.

The schematic reaction A+X→2XA+X\rightarrow2XA+X→2X captures the simplest amplification. Let aaa and xxx be the concentrations of supplied material AAA and catalyst XXX. With aaa fixed, a reaction-rate constant kkk, and a first-order loss rate ddd, mass-action kinetics gives x˙=(ka−d)x\dot x=(ka-d)xx˙=(ka−d)x. A small seed grows exponentially when ka>dka>dka>d and decays when losses dominate. In a closed vessel, consumption of AAA eventually removes the fixed-supply approximation. Continuous growth requires replenishment.

Lincoln and Joyce realized cross-catalytic replication with RNA. RNA is a chain molecule whose sequence can carry information and whose folded structure can catalyze reactions. Two RNA catalysts each joined supplied fragments to assemble copies of the other. Transfers into fresh substrate sustained amplification. This connects molecular reaction kinetics directly to the growth and competition of replicating populations.

A viable network must do more than contain a closed loop of reaction arrows. Production must outpace dilution and degradation, and side reactions must not consume essential intermediates too quickly. Hereditary evolution introduces a further requirement: differences between replicators must be transmitted and affect subsequent reproduction. Autocatalysis supplies amplification; the fidelity, resource supply, and physical organization of a particular system determine what can persist and evolve.

References
  • Lincoln & Joyce (2009), Self-sustained Replication of an RNA Enzyme. Demonstrates two RNA catalysts assembling copies of one another from supplied fragments, with continued amplification through substrate replenishment.
  • Hordijk & Steel (2012), Autocatalytic Sets Extended: Dynamics, Inhibition, and a Generalization. Analyzes molecular-flow dynamics and inhibition in networks satisfying autocatalytic-set criteria.

Back to contents ↑

45Homochirality: Amplification of molecular handedness

A chiral molecule cannot be superimposed on its mirror image by rotation. Its two mirror forms are called enantiomers. Proteins predominantly contain amino acids of one handedness, and the sugars in DNA and RNA also follow a consistent handedness preference. Chemistry can amplify an initial imbalance between mirror forms, but which processes established biological handedness remains a historical question.

Let LLL and DDD denote the concentrations of two enantiomers. Their enantiomeric excess is e=(L−D)/(L+D)e=(L-D)/(L+D)e=(L−D)/(L+D) for nonzero total concentration. Equal amounts give e=0e=0e=0; one pure form gives ∣e∣=1|e|=1∣e∣=1. Mirror-symmetric reaction equations can have an unstable symmetric solution and stable asymmetric ones. A fluctuation can then grow even though the equations favor neither sign. A small external bias can favor one branch.

One route combines autocatalysis—each form promotes its own production—with inhibition between opposite forms. Frank's reaction scheme made this mechanism explicit. The Soai reaction subsequently demonstrated amplification of a small enantiomeric excess in a laboratory chemical system. Whether an imbalance grows depends on the actual kinetics and catalyst interactions; autocatalysis by itself does not guarantee it.

Local symmetry breaking and a shared biological preference are different scales of the problem. Independently reacting compartments could choose opposite signs, so mixing their contents could reduce the net excess. A persistent preference must survive reproduction and exchange of material, and the handedness of interacting molecular families must remain compatible. Experiments establish that nonlinear chemistry can strongly amplify asymmetry. Connecting such a mechanism to the particular molecules and environments of early life requires additional evidence.

References
  • Soai et al. (1995), Asymmetric autocatalysis and amplification of enantiomeric excess of a chiral molecule. Demonstrates amplification of an initial enantiomeric excess in an asymmetric autocatalytic reaction.
  • Frank (1953), On spontaneous asymmetric synthesis. Introduces a reaction scheme in which autocatalysis and mutual inhibition destabilize a symmetric mixture.

Back to contents ↑

46Gene switches: Chemical feedback stores a cell state

A gene is a stretch of DNA used to produce a functional RNA or protein. Gene expression is the production of that molecule. Regulatory proteins can change expression by binding to DNA or to other components of the production machinery. Consequently, cells with the same DNA sequence can maintain different concentrations of gene products and behave differently.

Consider two proteins that repress each other's production. More AAA reduces BBB; less BBB releases AAA from repression. This double negative creates positive feedback. The circuit can maintain either high AAA and low BBB, or the reverse. Gardner, Cantor, and Collins built this arrangement in the bacterium Escherichia coli and used transient inputs to switch between persistent expression states.

A symmetric model is a˙=α/(1+bn)−a\dot a=\alpha/(1+b^n)-aa˙=α/(1+bn)−a and b˙=α/(1+an)−b\dot b=\alpha/(1+a^n)-bb˙=α/(1+an)−b. Concentrations a,ba,ba,b are measured relative to repression thresholds, and time in protein-loss times. The parameter α\alphaα sets maximum production and nnn the steepness of repression. Steady states occur where the two nullclines—the curves on which the respective derivatives vanish—intersect. Strong, steep repression can produce two stable asymmetric states separated by an unstable state. A perturbation that crosses the boundary between their basins changes the stored state.

Memory resides in the maintained concentration pattern. Individual proteins can be destroyed and replaced while the state persists, provided production compensates for losses and dilution as the cell grows. Molecular fluctuations can occasionally switch a small circuit, so the state's lifetime matters as well as its existence. Two reproducible long-lived states and their switching responses distinguish bistable memory from a single state that simply takes a long time to relax.

References
  • Gardner, Cantor & Collins (2000), Construction of a genetic toggle switch in Escherichia coli. Demonstrates an engineered two-repressor switch in E. coli and models the conditions supporting bistability.

Back to contents ↑

47Biological clocks: A daily rhythm from molecular reactions

A circadian clock is an internal oscillator with a period close to twenty-four hours. It continues to cycle under constant environmental conditions; daily light changes can adjust its phase, or position within the cycle. The period must therefore arise from internal dynamics, even when the environment helps keep the clock aligned with day and night.

In a particularly simple reconstruction, Nakajima and colleagues combined three proteins—KaiA, KaiB, and KaiC—with ATP. These proteins belong to cyanobacteria, bacteria that obtain energy from light. The mixture sustained daily oscillations in KaiC phosphorylation, the attachment of phosphate groups to that protein, outside a cell. Its period varied comparatively little with temperature over the tested range. ATP provided the chemical free energy needed to maintain the reaction cycle.

Different chemical states of KaiC interact differently with its partners. An ordered sequence of changes at two phosphorylation sites, together with delayed inhibitory interactions, allows activity to increase, suppress itself, and recover. This illustrates why internal state matters. A single autonomous variable obeying x˙=f(x)\dot x=f(x)x˙=f(x) cannot execute a nonconstant periodic orbit: once it returns to the same value, the same derivative applies. Several chemical states, or an effective delay, allow the system to return by a different route.

Bulk oscillation also requires coordination. If molecules cycle independently with fluctuating periods, their phases spread and the population average loses its rhythm. Shared binding partners and interactions can coordinate the cycles. Thus a biochemical clock involves both a molecular sequence of events and a population mechanism that keeps their timing coherent. The Kai system isolates these problems experimentally; other organisms use different molecular circuits to generate and regulate their daily rhythms.

References
  • Nakajima et al. (2005), Reconstitution of circadian oscillation of cyanobacterial KaiC phosphorylation in vitro. Reconstitutes KaiC phosphorylation rhythms with KaiA, KaiB, KaiC, and ATP, and examines temperature dependence and mutant periods.
  • Nishiwaki et al. (2007), A sequential program of dual phosphorylation of KaiC as a basis for circadian rhythm in cyanobacteria. Identifies the ordered cycle of changes at two KaiC phosphorylation sites and their relation to clock regulation.

Back to contents ↑

48Morphogenesis: From chemical gradients to biological form

Morphogenesis is the development of biological form through cell growth, movement, shape change, and organization. One early requirement is positional differentiation: different regions must activate different developmental programs. A morphogen is a chemical signal whose spatial distribution helps specify those responses. A concentration gradient can therefore translate physical position into differences in gene expression.

In an early fruit-fly embryo, the protein Bicoid forms a profile along the future head-to-tail direction and regulates other genes. At this stage many nuclei, the compartments containing DNA, share a common surrounding cellular material. Gregor and colleagues measured Bicoid concentrations, their fluctuations, and the response of a target gene. This made the precision of positional signaling a quantitative problem.

As a simple model, suppose a signal is supplied at one end of a long one-dimensional domain, diffuses with coefficient DDD, and is removed at rate μ\muμ. Away from the source, a steady profile obeys Dc′′−μc=0Dc''-\mu c=0Dc′′−μc=0. With c(0)=c0c(0)=c_0c(0)=c0​ and decay far from the source, c(x)=c0e−x/λc(x)=c_0e^{-x/\lambda}c(x)=c0​e−x/λ, where λ=D/μ\lambda=\sqrt{D/\mu}λ=D/μ​. A threshold response at concentration c∗c_*c∗​ gives a boundary x∗=λln⁡(c0/c∗)x_* =\lambda\ln(c_0/c_*)x∗​=λln(c0​/c∗​). This illustrative model shows both how a length scale arises and why a change in source strength shifts the boundary.

The boundary also fluctuates because signal molecules arrive and bind randomly. Averaging over time or nearby regions, and interactions among regulatory genes, can improve reproducibility. Subsequent tissue mechanics determines how the chemical pattern becomes shape: cells exert forces and rearrange. Establishing a signal profile, interpreting it reliably, and mechanically realizing the resulting organization are distinct stages of the same developmental process.

References
  • Gregor et al. (2007), Probing the limits to positional information. Measures Bicoid concentrations, fluctuations, target-gene responses, and reproducibility among embryos; the exponential profile here is an illustrative model.

49Cellular homeostasis: Feedback maintains a stable cellular output

Homeostasis is the maintenance of internal conditions through ongoing physiological processes. A stable output can coexist with rapid molecular turnover. The central dynamical question is how the output returns after a disturbance, even if the disturbance persists or reaction rates vary.

Bacterial chemotaxis provides a tractable example. Chemotaxis is movement biased by chemical conditions; bacteria change their swimming behavior when an attractant concentration changes. After a sustained change, their signaling activity can return close to its previous level, leaving the system responsive to further changes. Chemical modification of receptors, molecules that detect the attractant, supplies a slowly changing internal variable. Barkai and Leibler modeled this robust adaptation, and Yi and colleagues related it to integral feedback control.

Let yyy be the regulated output and let an internal variable zzz obey z˙=k(y0−y)\dot z=k(y_0-y)z˙=k(y0​−y), with k>0k>0k>0. The value of zzz accumulates the discrepancy between yyy and a reference value y0y_0y0​, and feeds back on the processes controlling yyy. At a stable steady state with finite zzz, the condition z˙=0\dot z=0z˙=0 requires y=y0y=y_0y=y0​. A constant disturbance changes the necessary controller state while leaving the output at the reference value. The result follows from the form of the feedback equation.

Its assumptions identify the operating limits. A controller with a bounded range cannot compensate for an arbitrarily large disturbance. Loss of the stored control variable can leave a residual error, and poorly matched response times can destabilize the feedback. Within its operating range, however, the circuit maintains a predictable response despite changes in its molecular components. In chemotaxis, the maintained quantity is a signaling activity; adaptation does not mean that every internal concentration remains fixed.

References
  • Barkai & Leibler (1997), Robustness in simple biochemical networks. Shows how a chemotaxis network can achieve adaptation that is robust to changes in model parameters.
  • Yi et al. (2000), Robust perfect adaptation in bacterial chemotaxis through integral feedback control. Connects chemotactic adaptation to integral feedback and identifies the conditions needed for exact steady-state adaptation.

50Multicellularity: A cluster acquires a reproducing life cycle

Multicellularity ranges from loose cell associations to organisms whose cells depend on one another. An important evolutionary step occurs when a group grows, produces descendant groups, and transmits traits of its organization. At that point, differences among groups can affect which group forms become more common.

Ratcliff and colleagues observed this process in yeast, single-celled fungi that reproduce by budding off daughter cells. They repeatedly transferred the rapidly settling portion of a culture. Cells evolved persistent attachment after division, producing branching clusters. Cluster size affected settling, and fragmentation produced smaller clusters capable of further growth. A cellular change thus generated a collective physical property that altered success under the imposed selection procedure.

Selection among groups requires heritable variation in group reproductive success. For example, groups might differ in the size at which they fragment; this difference might affect how many surviving descendant groups they produce; and descendants might resemble the parent in that trait. These conditions make a group trait evolve. Growth of a single cluster alone would establish none of the comparisons needed to show this.

Cellular and group reproduction need not favor the same changes. Faster division within a cluster can interfere with transport or mechanical integrity, whereas reduced reproduction by some cells can support collective maintenance. Development from closely related cells can reduce internal genetic conflict, and specialization can make cells increasingly dependent on the group. The yeast experiment captures an early route into this organization: repeated attachment, growth, and fragmentation connect a physical boundary to a heritable life cycle. More elaborate multicellular organisms build on additional mechanisms for development, coordination, and conflict control.

References
  • Ratcliff et al. (2012), Experimental evolution of multicellularity. Documents settling selection, persistent attachment after cell division, cluster reproduction, and evolved group traits in snowflake yeast.

Back to contents ↑

Chapter 6

Ecology and evolution: collectives with histories

Ecology studies organisms' interactions with one another and their environment. Evolution concerns changes in inherited characteristics across generations. The two are coupled: organisms alter resources and competitors, while these conditions affect which organisms reproduce. Collective behavior therefore depends on both present interactions and the history that produced them.

We begin with selection, evolutionary innovation, cooperation, and task allocation. Flocking then provides an example of organization on a much shorter time scale, as individuals coordinate their motion without evolving during the event. The remaining entries consider communities: the stability of interaction networks, recovery from disturbance, succession, infection spread, and the exchange of nutrients between microbes. Simple models identify mechanisms and measurable quantities. Experiments determine which of those mechanisms matter in a particular population or environment.

51Natural selection: Heritable differences change a population

Natural selection occurs when heritable differences affect reproductive success. Heritable means that descendants tend to retain the relevant differences. If one bacterial variant leaves more descendants in a nutrient solution, its share of the population can increase even though no individual improves during its lifetime. Fitness measures reproductive contribution under specified conditions; it depends on the environment and on the other organisms present.

For two faithfully inherited variants, let ppp be the frequency of type AAA and let wA,wBw_A,w_BwA​,wB​ be their expected numbers of descendants. In a deterministic generation model, p′=pwA/[pwA+(1−p)wB]p'=p w_A/[p w_A+(1-p)w_B]p′=pwA​/[pwA​+(1−p)wB​]. Thus AAA increases when wA>wBw_A>w_BwA​>wB​. This is an accounting relation once reproductive rates are specified. Resource use, survival, and interactions explain those rates and why their ordering can change.

In Lenski and Travisano's long-term experiment, replicate bacterial populations adapted to the same laboratory conditions over ten thousand generations while diverging from one another. Repeated exposure to the same conditions produced a common direction of adaptation without fixing a unique genetic route. Mutations—changes in hereditary sequence—supply new variation. Genetic drift adds random changes in variant frequencies through finite sampling of reproduction and survival.

Adaptation is the improved fit to particular conditions that selection can produce. It need not increase every measure of performance: using one resource more efficiently may reduce performance on another, and a variant's advantage may disappear as it becomes common. Nor is every frequent trait adaptive. A neutral difference can spread because it is inherited together with a beneficial one. The population-level outcome is a changing distribution of traits, shaped jointly by selective differences, chance, and the available hereditary variation.

References
  • Lenski & Travisano (1994), Dynamics of adaptation and diversification: a 10,000-generation experiment with bacterial populations. Measures adaptation relative to an ancestor and divergence among replicate E. coli populations over ten thousand generations.

Back to contents ↑

52Evolutionary innovation: New capabilities depend on evolutionary history

An evolutionary innovation is a capability or organization absent from a lineage's ancestors. It can arise by changing when an existing component is used or by combining components differently. The effect of a new mutation therefore depends on the system in which it occurs, making the route to a capability part of its explanation.

The long-term Escherichia coli experiment offers a concrete case. Its medium contained citrate, a carbon-containing molecule that the ancestral bacteria could not use as a carbon source under the experiment's oxygenated conditions. One population evolved that ability. Blount, Borland, and Lenski restarted evolution from stored samples and found that later genetic backgrounds were more likely to produce citrate-using descendants. Molecular work then identified changes that enabled and refined the new metabolism, the chemical transformations supporting growth and maintenance.

We can represent the dependence using two genetic changes, aaa and bbb. If the effect of bbb differs according to whether aaa is present, the changes exhibit epistasis. Their effects cannot be treated as independent contributions. A useful combination may become accessible after an earlier change that originally spread for another reason. Equal current growth rates therefore need not imply equal access to future capabilities.

Think of hereditary sequences as vertices of a graph, with edges joining sequences accessible by one mutational step. Reproduction and loss determine which routes are occupied, while the environment changes the advantage of moving along them. Physical chemistry constrains the possible endpoints, but intermediate states constrain which endpoints a lineage can reach. Replaying evolution from preserved ancestors makes this historical dependence experimentally testable: it compares the distribution of subsequent outcomes from different starting backgrounds.

References
  • Blount, Borland & Lenski (2008), Historical contingency and the evolution of a key innovation in an experimental population of Escherichia coli. Uses replay experiments from preserved bacterial populations to test how prior evolution changes access to citrate use.
  • Quandt et al. (2015), Fine-tuning citrate synthase flux potentiates and refines metabolic innovation in the Lenski evolution experiment. Identifies changes in citrate synthase activity that contributed to the preparation for, and refinement of, citrate-use metabolism.

Back to contents ↑

53Cooperation: A shared resource can sustain its producers

A cell may release an enzyme that makes food available to its neighbors. If producing the enzyme is costly, a nonproducer can benefit without contributing. Cooperation in evolutionary biology concerns effects that benefit another organism, assessed through reproduction; costly cooperation poses the additional problem of explaining why contributors persist in competition with noncontributors.

Yeast growing on sucrose provide a well-studied case. The enzyme invertase splits sucrose near the cell surface, and much of the resulting food diffuses away. In experiments by Gore and colleagues, producing cells retained a small direct benefit. Combined with a nonlinear relationship between available food and growth, this allowed producers and nonproducers each to increase when rare under suitable conditions. Neither type eliminated the other.

Let ppp be the producer fraction and fP(p),fN(p)f_P(p),f_N(p)fP​(p),fN​(p) their respective per-capita growth rates. Then p˙=p(1−p)[fP(p)−fN(p)]\dot p=p(1-p)[f_P(p)-f_N(p)]p˙​=p(1−p)[fP​(p)−fN​(p)]. If producers do better when rare but worse when common, a crossing of the two rates from positive to negative difference gives a stable mixed population. The maintained producer fraction follows from the dependence of growth on composition.

Spatial arrangement changes this dependence by determining who receives the released material. Limited diffusion can keep benefits near producers, while mixing spreads them more widely. Relatedness and repeated interactions can also alter how benefits return to contributors, but each requires a specified biological mechanism. Population productivity and resistance to invasion are separate outcomes: the mixture with the highest total yield need not be evolutionarily stable. Measuring both individual growth and shared-resource flows explains which cooperative arrangements can persist.

References
  • Gore, Youk & van Oudenaarden (2009), Snowdrift game dynamics and facultative cheating in yeast. Shows frequency-dependent coexistence of invertase producers and nonproducers, linked to nonlinear growth benefits and partial retention of released food.
  • Ohtsuki et al. (2006), A simple rule for the evolution of cooperation on graphs and social networks. Derives cooperation criteria for specified interaction graphs, selection strengths, and population update rules.

54Division of labor: Task specialization among similar individuals

Division of labor occurs when different individuals consistently perform different activities. Fixed differences in anatomy can create specialists, but similar individuals can also specialize through their interactions and experience. The relevant observation is persistence across time: a single snapshot of workers doing different things establishes only that several tasks are underway.

Consider an illustrative colony with food collection and care of young. Unfinished work increases a task signal, and a worker begins the task when that signal exceeds its response threshold. Completed work reduces the signal, limiting further recruitment. If performing a task also lowers that worker's threshold for it, small initial differences can grow into persistent specialization. Local responses to demand then allocate effort without requiring any individual to monitor the whole colony.

Ulrich and colleagues tested groups of clonal raider ants whose workers were closely matched in age and genetically alike. Larger groups developed stronger and more persistent differences in activity, even at small group sizes. Colony conditions became more stable and reproductive performance improved. Their model attributed much of the increased stability to group size itself and a smaller contribution to specialization. Thus the experiment and model distinguish the coexistence of two changes from the claim that one fully explains the other.

The strength of reinforcement creates a tradeoff. Persistent roles can reduce task switching, but workers must sometimes replace absent specialists or respond to new demand. Removing workers from a task and measuring how the remaining group reallocates effort tests this flexibility. The collective property is the distribution and persistence of task participation, together with its response to changing workload.

References
  • Ulrich et al. (2018), Fitness benefits and emergent division of labour at the onset of group living. Tracks specialization in clonal ant groups and uses a model to separate effects of group size and division of labor on colony stability.

Back to contents ↑

55Collective motion: Local interactions coordinate a moving group

A flock can turn coherently even though each bird observes only part of the group. To isolate the coordination problem, we can model individuals as self-propelled particles that continuously use energy to move. Interactions align their headings, regulate separation, or avoid collisions. A common direction then becomes a property of the coupled trajectories.

In the Vicsek alignment model, each particle adopts the direction of the vector sum of its neighbors' headings, adds a random angular perturbation, and moves forward. This circular average avoids treating headings just below and above 2π2\pi2π as opposites. Polarization, P=∣∑ivi∣/∑i∣vi∣P=|\sum_i\mathbf v_i|/\sum_i|\mathbf v_i|P=∣∑i​vi​∣/∑i​∣vi​∣, measures directional order. Aligned velocities give P≃1P\simeq1P≃1; random headings in a large group largely cancel. Varying noise, density, and interactions changes whether ordered motion persists.

Which individuals count as neighbors is experimentally consequential. Ballerini and colleagues reconstructed starling flocks in three dimensions and found spatial structure consistent with an interaction range set by neighbor rank, rather than a single fixed physical distance. Such a rule can preserve connections as a flock expands or compresses. The result is evidence about the observed flocks, while other species and circumstances may involve different interaction rules.

Large polarization alone cannot distinguish social coordination from independent responses to wind, light, or another common cue. The propagation of a turn, including delays and changing neighbor relationships, supplies additional evidence. This connects the visible group pattern to the information available locally. Directional order, rapid collective turning, and resistance to fragmentation are measurable outcomes whose dependence on the interaction rule can be tested separately.

References
  • Ballerini et al. (2008), Interaction ruling animal collective behavior depends on topological rather than metric distance: Evidence from a field study. Infers a neighbor-rank interaction range from three-dimensional starling flock structure and compares cohesion under alternative model rules.
  • Vicsek et al. (1995), Novel type of phase transition in a system of self-driven particles. Demonstrates collective directional order in a minimal model of moving particles with local alignment and angular noise.

56Food webs: Interaction structure controls community stability

A food web records which organisms consume which others. Extra species and links can provide alternative resource pathways, but they also introduce routes through which disturbances spread. Their effect on stability depends on interaction strengths and organization, rather than on the number of species alone.

Write population dynamics as n˙i=fi(n)\dot n_i=f_i(\mathbf n)n˙i​=fi​(n), where nin_ini​ is the abundance of species iii. Near an equilibrium n∗\mathbf n_*n∗​, small deviations obey δn˙=Jδn\dot{\delta\mathbf n}=J\delta\mathbf nδn˙=Jδn, with Jij=∂fi/∂njJ_{ij}=\partial f_i/\partial n_jJij​=∂fi​/∂nj​ evaluated at that equilibrium. Negative real parts of all eigenvalues ensure local asymptotic stability; a positive real part implies instability. Zero real parts require nonlinear analysis. A predator-prey pair typically produces opposite signs in its two off-diagonal entries: more prey benefits the predator, while more predators harm the prey.

May's random-matrix analysis gave a useful comparison. Suppose diagonal entries are −d-d−d, and off-diagonal interactions are independently present with probability CCC, have zero mean, and have variance σ2\sigma^2σ2 when present. For a large matrix of SSS species, the random eigenvalue spectrum extends roughly σSC\sigma\sqrt{SC}σSC​ from its center at −d-d−d. Stability is lost near σSC=d\sigma\sqrt{SC}=dσSC​=d. Correlations between reciprocal interactions change that spectrum, as Allesina and Tang showed for different interaction types.

This is a statement about an ensemble of linearized models. A coexistence equilibrium must also be feasible, with positive abundances, and a locally stable state may fail after a large disturbance. Real communities are assembled through colonization, competition, and evolution, which impose structure absent from independent random entries. The random model is valuable because it identifies what needs explanation: correlations and constraints that alter collective growth and decay modes.

References
  • May (1972), Will a Large Complex System be Stable?. Derives a local stability criterion for large random community matrices with stabilizing diagonal terms.
  • Allesina & Tang (2012), Stability criteria for complex ecosystems. Shows how correlations in the signs and strengths of reciprocal interactions change random-matrix stability criteria.

57Ecosystem resilience: Recovery rates and the size of a disturbance

Two ecosystems can have similar present conditions but respond very differently to the same disturbance. An ecosystem includes a community of organisms and its physical and chemical environment. Resilience can mean rapid recovery after a small disturbance, or the ability to withstand a large disturbance without switching to a different persistent regime. These properties need not change together.

For local recovery, write δx˙=−rδx\dot{\delta x}=-r\delta xδx˙=−rδx with r>0r>0r>0. The return time is 1/r1/r1/r. Near a bifurcation at which this recovery rate vanishes, disturbances decay increasingly slowly. If stationary white noise drives the linear system at fixed strength, its variance and temporal correlations increase as well. Changing noise strength or external forcing can produce similar statistics, so fluctuations alone do not identify the cause.

Experiments can directly test the disturbance response. Veraart and colleagues increased light levels toward a collapse threshold in cyanobacteria, bacteria that obtain energy through photosynthesis. Recovery from small disturbances slowed as the threshold approached. In a whole-lake experiment, Carpenter and colleagues observed warning statistics during food-web reorganization induced by adding top predators, using a reference lake for comparison.

Resistance to larger disturbances concerns the geometry beyond the linear neighborhood. If two stable regimes have different basins of attraction—the sets of states that return to each—a disturbance can carry the system across their boundary. A state may recover quickly from tiny displacements while lying close to that boundary. Measuring both recovery rates and the disturbances needed to trigger persistent change separates these meanings of resilience. It also explains why a sudden external shock can cause a transition without a preceding trend of slower recovery.

References
  • Carpenter et al. (2011), Early warnings of regime shifts: a whole-ecosystem experiment. Reports warning statistics during a manipulated lake food-web transition, with a reference lake for comparison.
  • Veraart et al. (2012), Recovery rates reflect distance to a tipping point in a living system. Tests recovery rates and temporal correlations in cyanobacterial populations approaching a light-induced collapse threshold.

58Ecological succession: Community change depends on earlier occupants

Ecological succession is change in the species composition of a community through time, often after a disturbance. A community consists of the populations of different species living together. Early arrivals can alter light, nutrients, space, and other conditions, changing which organisms can subsequently establish.

Connell and Slatyer distinguished three mechanisms. In facilitation, early occupants improve conditions for later species. In inhibition, they prevent or delay establishment by occupying space or consuming resources. In tolerance, later species can establish without this assistance and eventually persist because they tolerate conditions that exclude earlier occupants. Different mechanisms can operate at different stages or between different species pairs.

A simple approximation exposes the causal question. Let EEE be the abundance of an early colonist and let a rare later species have per-capita growth gL=rL+aEg_L=r_L+aEgL​=rL​+aE. Positive aaa represents facilitation, negative aaa inhibition, and a≃0a\simeq0a≃0 little direct effect in this approximation. The fact that one species appears first does not determine aaa: both species may respond independently to changing soil or weather. Experiments that add or remove early occupants, while accounting for the disturbance caused by the intervention, can distinguish these possibilities.

Arrival also depends on dispersal, the movement of organisms or reproductive material between places. Suitable conditions do not guarantee that a species has reached the site. Different arrival orders can therefore produce different communities under otherwise similar conditions. Repeated disturbance may prevent a persistent endpoint, and a changing environment can alter which endpoints are possible. Succession is a trajectory of interacting populations and their surroundings; explaining it requires the effects of earlier occupants as well as the conditions observed today.

References
  • Connell & Slatyer (1977), Mechanisms of Succession in Natural Communities and Their Role in Community Stability and Organization. Formulates facilitation, tolerance, and inhibition as alternative mechanisms of succession and identifies ways to distinguish them.

59Epidemics: Transmission produces a population threshold

An infection can disappear after a few transmissions or spread through a substantial fraction of a population. The outcome depends on susceptible hosts, contact patterns, and infectiousness. A simple population model shows how these ingredients generate a threshold that no isolated infected individual possesses.

In the susceptible-infectious-removed model, SSS, III, and RRR count individuals who can acquire infection, can transmit it, and no longer participate in transmission. Assume a closed population of size NNN, homogeneous mixing, effective contact rate β\betaβ, and removal rate γ\gammaγ. Then S˙=−βSI/N\dot S=-\beta SI/NS˙=−βSI/N, I˙=βSI/N−γI\dot I=\beta SI/N-\gamma II˙=βSI/N−γI, and R˙=γI\dot R=\gamma IR˙=γI. Removal can represent recovery with immunity over the modeled interval. These constant-rate equations are a special case of the epidemic theory developed by Kermack and McKendrick.

Initially, infection grows when βS/N>γ\beta S/N>\gammaβS/N>γ. In a fully susceptible population, the basic reproduction number R0=β/γR_0=\beta/\gammaR0​=β/γ is the expected number of secondary infections caused by one infectious individual under these assumptions. As susceptibles are depleted, the effective value R0S/NR_0S/NR0​S/N falls. The infectious population peaks when it crosses one, while many susceptible individuals can still remain. Transmission then continues at a declining rate.

The deterministic threshold describes average growth, while early transmissions in a finite population are random. Even with R0>1R_0>1R0​>1, an introduction can die out. In a population divided into interacting groups, a next-generation matrix records the expected secondary infections between groups; its dominant eigenvalue determines the invasion threshold. The exponential growth rate in time also depends on when transmissions occur. Thus reproduction number, outbreak probability, and growth speed are related but distinct quantities, each requiring the relevant contact and timing assumptions.

References
  • Kermack & McKendrick (1927), A contribution to the mathematical theory of epidemics. Develops epidemic thresholds in a formulation that includes the time since infection; constant-rate SIR is a special case.
  • Kermack & McKendrick (1991 reprint), Contributions to the mathematical theory of epidemics—I. 1927. Reprints the original epidemic theory, including its homogeneous-population assumptions and threshold behavior.
  • Diekmann, Heesterbeek & Roberts (2010), The construction of next-generation matrices for compartmental epidemic models. Constructs next-generation matrices and distinguishes reproduction number from exponential growth rate in time.

60Microbiome mutualism: Resource exchange creates community capabilities

Microbial communities contain organisms with different metabolic capabilities. Metabolism is the set of chemical transformations supporting growth and maintenance. In cross-feeding, material released by one organism becomes a resource for another. A community can therefore process substances, or sustain members, that would not be supported by the same organisms in isolation.

Suppose bacterium AAA breaks a large food molecule into fragments that bacterium BBB absorbs. This establishes a flow of material from AAA to BBB, but a benefit to BBB alone does not establish mutualism, a relationship benefiting both partners. The distinction requires comparisons of growth or persistence with and without the partner, together with interventions on the proposed exchange.

Rakoff-Nahoum and colleagues studied this distinction in gut bacteria. Bacteroides ovatus can break down inulin, a dietary chain of sugar units, outside the cell. The released products support Bacteroides vulgatus. Disabling the relevant digestive enzymes and comparing cultures and defined communities in mice showed that the producer gained a competitive benefit from the partner's presence under the tested conditions. The exact mechanism of the return benefit was not fully resolved. Other digestive systems in the same study largely retained their benefits within the producing cells.

These interactions depend on resource supply, diffusion, uptake, and competition. A partner's effect can change with the available food or with the other species present. Consequently, a community's rate of resource processing must be measured under specified conditions. A species list or a correlation between abundances cannot determine the underlying exchange: both organisms might simply respond to the same diet. The collective capability follows from the causal network of transformations and transfers.

References
  • Rakoff-Nahoum, Foster & Comstock (2016), The evolution of cooperation within the gut microbiota. Uses enzyme deletions, cultures, and communities in mice to test cross-feeding and reciprocal competitive benefits between gut bacteria.

Chapter 7

Brains: collective dynamics and the limits of explanation

Neurons are cells specialized for electrical and chemical signaling. Their interactions support activity on many scales, from a voltage pulse along one cell to patterns distributed across a network. This chapter follows those scales through rhythms, sensory representation, memory, decisions, learning, and navigation.

Some mechanisms, such as the ionic currents underlying an action potential, have a detailed physical account. Others are best understood through models that show how a computation could occur. Recordings and interventions connect those models to biology: extracting a variable from neural activity shows that the activity contains information about it, while changing the activity tests its contribution to behavior.

The final entries examine two open problems. Neural criticality asks whether collective activity lies near a particular dynamical transition. Consciousness asks how neural organization relates to subjective experience. In both cases, progress depends on specifying which observations a proposed explanation predicts and how competing explanations differ.

61Action potentials: Ion channels generate a traveling electrical pulse

A neuron is a cell specialized for electrical and chemical signaling. Its membrane separates fluids containing ions, electrically charged atoms or molecules. Membrane proteins called ion channels selectively allow these ions to pass. An action potential is a brief change in membrane voltage that regenerates as it travels, allowing a signal to propagate much farther than a passive pulse on a leaky membrane.

In the classic sodium-potassium mechanism, making the cell interior less negative opens sodium channels. Sodium entry raises the voltage further and opens more channels: positive feedback. Sodium-channel inactivation and delayed opening of potassium channels end the rise and repolarize the membrane. The ensuing refractory period, during which another spike is harder or impossible to initiate, separates successive events. Hodgkin and Huxley connected these processes quantitatively to measurements on the squid's large axon, the long cell extension along which signals travel.

The local current balance is CmV˙=Iext−∑aga(V,t)(V−Ea)C_m\dot V=I_{\rm ext}-\sum_a g_a(V,t)(V-E_a)Cm​V˙=Iext​−∑a​ga​(V,t)(V−Ea​). Here VVV is the voltage inside relative to outside, CmC_mCm​ is capacitance per membrane area, and IextI_{\rm ext}Iext​ is applied current per area. Each gag_aga​ is a conductance per area, changing as channels open and close; EaE_aEa​ is its reversal potential, where the ionic current changes direction. Current between adjacent membrane segments allows an excited segment to initiate the same process in its neighbor.

The propagating object is a coordinated voltage wave involving many channels. It does not require the same ions to travel the length of the axon. Chemical-energy-consuming pumps maintain the ionic concentration differences over longer times, while channel gating drives the rapid spike. Channel types and cell geometry determine the resulting wave shape, speed, and reliability.

References
  • Hodgkin & Huxley (1952), A quantitative description of membrane current and its application to conduction and excitation in nerve. Relates measured squid-axon ionic conductances to membrane excitation and action-potential propagation.
  • Gerstner et al. (2014), Neuronal Dynamics, section 2.2: Hodgkin–Huxley Model. Derives capacitive membrane dynamics and explains sodium and potassium gating, propagation prerequisites, and refractory behavior.

62Neural oscillations: Excitation and inhibition generate a network rhythm

A population of neurons can oscillate even when its individual cells do not behave as autonomous clocks. Neurons communicate through synapses, connections that change the receiving cell's electrical state. Excitatory input promotes firing, while inhibitory input suppresses it in the operating regime considered here. Their interaction can create a repeating cycle of activation and suppression.

Let EEE and III be average activities of excitatory and inhibitory populations. A simplified rate model is τEE˙=−E+F(wEEE−wEII+P)\tau_E\dot E=-E+F(w_{EE}E-w_{EI}I+P)τE​E˙=−E+F(wEE​E−wEI​I+P) and τII˙=−I+F(wIEE−wIII+Q)\tau_I\dot I=-I+F(w_{IE}E-w_{II}I+Q)τI​I˙=−I+F(wIE​E−wII​I+Q). Positive coefficients www set coupling strengths, P,QP,QP,Q are external drives, τE,τI\tau_E,\tau_IτE​,τI​ are response times, and FFF maps total input to bounded activity. Excitation recruits inhibition; inhibition reduces excitation; reduced excitation then allows inhibition to fall. Suitable response times and gains make this cycle self-sustaining.

Wilson and Cowan showed how population models can support steady states, switching, and stable limit cycles—periodic trajectories that attract nearby states. The equations here simplify that approach. Oscillatory eigenvalues near a steady state identify a possible rhythm and its damping or growth, but the nonlinear dynamics determines whether an attracting cycle exists.

A measured oscillation may instead be a damped response repeatedly excited by input, or a response to periodic external forcing. Its persistence after a drive is removed helps distinguish these cases. Population rhythms also need not require every cell to fire on every cycle: changes in the fraction of active neurons can generate a strong bulk signal. Connecting a rhythm to behavior requires a further step, such as changing its timing or coupling and measuring the resulting performance. Frequency alone does not specify what a network computes.

References
  • Wilson & Cowan (1972), Excitatory and inhibitory interactions in localized populations of model neurons. Demonstrates steady states, multiple stable states, and limit cycles in interacting excitatory and inhibitory populations.
  • Gerstner et al. (2014), Neuronal Dynamics, section 20.2: Oscillations: good or bad?. Explains network oscillations, their relation to single-cell firing, and the stability of asynchronous population activity.

63Population coding: A variable is represented across many neurons

A neuron's firing rate is the number of electrical spikes it produces per unit time. A tuning curve describes how its average rate changes with a stimulus or behavior. A cell might fire most strongly during a northeastward reach while also responding to nearby directions. Its rate alone is therefore ambiguous. A population code uses the joint activity of many neurons to represent the variable more precisely.

Suppose neuron iii has preferred direction ui\mathbf u_iui​, a unit vector, and measured firing rate rir_iri​. A population-vector decoder forms p=∑i(ri−ri,0)ui\mathbf p=\sum_i(r_i-r_{i,0})\mathbf u_ip=∑i​(ri​−ri,0​)ui​, with baseline rates ri,0r_{i,0}ri,0​. For uniformly distributed preferences and matching cosine-like tuning, components transverse to the movement cancel and the vector points along it. Georgopoulos and colleagues found that population vectors tracked reach direction in recordings from primate motor cortex, a brain region involved in movement.

Combining responses can also reduce uncertainty. Independent fluctuations average down as more informative neurons are included. Shared fluctuations behave differently: if they change the population pattern in the same way as a change in the stimulus, no decoder can reliably tell the two apart. The pattern of correlations relative to the tuning curves matters more than whether correlations are simply positive or negative.

A decoder is an explicit rule for extracting information from activity. Its success establishes that the variable is recoverable under the tested conditions. To explain the brain's computation, we must also determine how other neurons use that information and how perturbing the population affects behavior. The useful collective description is therefore the geometry and variability of the joint response, with respect to a specified stimulus or task.

References
  • Georgopoulos, Kettner & Schwartz (1988), Primate motor cortex and free arm movements to visual targets in three-dimensional space. II. Coding of the direction of movement by a neuronal population. Tests population-vector estimates of three-dimensional reach direction using directionally tuned motor-cortex neurons.
  • Moreno-Bote et al. (2014), Information-limiting correlations. Shows how noise correlations that resemble changes in the encoded variable can limit information in a neural population.

64Attractor memory: Network dynamics completes a stored pattern

Content-addressable memory retrieves a pattern from a similar or incomplete cue, rather than from a numerical storage address. A dynamical implementation makes each stored pattern an attractor: nearby network states evolve toward it. Errors in the cue can then be corrected through interactions among the units.

In a Hopfield network, unit iii has binary state si=±1s_i=\pm1si​=±1. Define its local input as hi=∑jwijsj−θih_i=\sum_jw_{ij}s_j-\theta_ihi​=∑j​wij​sj​−θi​, where wijw_{ij}wij​ are connection weights and θi\theta_iθi​ is a threshold. For symmetric weights and no self-couplings, the function E=−12∑ijwijsisj+∑iθisiE=-\tfrac12\sum_{ij}w_{ij}s_is_j+\sum_i\theta_i s_iE=−21​∑ij​wij​si​sj​+∑i​θi​si​ decreases whenever a unit changes to agree with a nonzero hih_ihi​. Repeatedly visiting every unit, updating one at a time, and leaving it unchanged when hi=0h_i=0hi​=0 leads a finite network to a fixed point. This is a mathematical energy for the update rule.

A simple storage prescription is wij=N−1∑μξiμξjμw_{ij}=N^{-1}\sum_\mu\xi_i^\mu\xi_j^\muwij​=N−1∑μ​ξiμ​ξjμ​ for i≠ji\ne ji=j, where NNN is the number of units and ξμ\xi^\muξμ are the patterns. The resulting connections reinforce agreements present across the stored patterns. Hopfield's model showed how suitable patterns and sufficiently informative cues can produce reliable completion through collective relaxation.

Each attractor has a basin: the starting states that converge to it. A damaged cue is corrected only while it remains in the appropriate basin. Too many or strongly correlated stored patterns cause interference, and unintended fixed points can appear. Simultaneous updates or asymmetric weights also remove the stated energy-descent guarantee. This model makes a specific memory mechanism understandable: distributed connections create robust retrieval regions, and retrieval errors arise when the cue or the stored associations send the dynamics into the wrong region.

References
  • Hopfield (1982), Neural networks and physical systems with emergent collective computational abilities. Introduces distributed pattern storage and retrieval through collective dynamics, with convergence under the specified symmetric asynchronous update rule.
  • Gerstner et al. (2014), Neuronal Dynamics, section 17.2: Hopfield Model. Derives energy descent and explains retrieval, storage limits, and unintended fixed points in Hopfield networks.
